H Ow dearely welcome you are! You may Sir, For all ſhe is, is yours. Ile pawne my life on't And this is he; Come hither Miſtris Dorothy, And Miſtris Mary: who do's that face looke like: And view my brother well?
I know it, And my beſt ſiſter, you as deer to my ſight, And pray let this confirm it, how you have govern'd My poore ſtate in my abſence, how my ſervants, I dare and muſt beleeve, elſe I ſhould wrong ye, The beſt and worthieſt. For the poore boyes loſſe, I have brought a noble friend, I found in travell A worthier minde, and a more temperate ſpirit If J have ſo much judgement to diſcerne 'em, Man yet was never maſter of. A Gentleman, I doe aſſure my ſelfe, And of a worthy breeding, though he hide it: I found him at Valentia, poore and needy, Onely his minde the maſter of a treaſure. I ſought his friendſhip, wonne him by much violence, His honeſty and modeſty ſtill fearing To thruſt a charge upon me; how I love him, He ſhall now know, where want and he hereafter Shall be no more companions: uſe him nobly, It is my will, good ſiſter, all I have J make him free companion in, and part er, But onely What, Monſieur Hylas, I 'me glad to ſee your merry body well yet. None, but new men expected, ſuch as you are To breed new admirations: 'tis my ſiſter, Pray ye know her ſir. What, the old ſquire of dames ſtill? My loving, and kind coſin, A thouſand welcomes. I thanke • e: But wher's my bleſſed Cellide? her ſlackneſſe In viſitation. Ye have given me too much comfort. It is ſo, and a bait you cannot balke ſir, If your old rule raigne in you, ye may know her. A happy ſtocke ye have, right worthy Lady, The pooreſt of your ſervants, vowes his duty And obliged faith. O my deere life, my better heart, all dangers, Diſtreſſes in my travell, all misfortunes, Had they been endleſſe like the houres upon me, In this kiſſe, had been buried in oblivion: How happy have ye made me, truely happy? O deereſt: My noble friend too: what a bleſſedneſſe Have I about me now? how full my wiſhes Are come agen, a thouſand hearty welcomes I once more lay upon ye: all I have, The faire and liberall uſe of all my ſervants To be at your command, and all the uſes Of al within my power. Ye wrong my tender love now, even my ſervice, Nothing accepted, nothing ſtuck between us And our intire affections, but this woman, This I beſeech ye friend. Yes: with me Sir. A great deale better: Why doe you bluſh? the Gentleman will doe well. How do's his Father? The ayre, The ſharpe and nipping ayre of our new clymat I hope is all, which will as well reſtore To health againe th'affected body by it, And make it ſtronger far, as leave it dangerous; How do's my ſweet, our bleſſed houre comes on now Apace my Cellide, (it knocks at dore) In which our loves, and long deſires like rivers Riſing aſunder far, ſhall fall together, Within theſe too daies deere. He ſweats extreamely: Hot, very hot: his pulſe beats like a drum now, Feele ſiſter, feele, feele ſweet. My gowne there. This is moſt unhappy, Take courage man, 'tis nothing but an ague. May all I have reſtore him? So deerely and ſo tenderly I love him, I doe not know the cauſe why, yea my life too. 'Twas that I onely fear'd: good friend go from me, I finde my heart too full for further conference: You are aſſur'd of this? I ſhall do, and I thank ye: pray ye no words on't, I doe not uſe to talke ſir. Exit. Goe comfort him deere ſiſter. Exit Alice. And one word ſweet, with you: then we'l go to him. What think you of this Gentleman? It is indeed: but Cellide, he muſt dye. He may, but with much danger: my ſweet Cellide You have a powerfull tongue. J will betray his griefe: he loves a gentlewoman, A friend of yours, whoſe heart another holds, He knowes it too: yet ſuch a ſway blinde fancy, And his not daring to deliver it, Have won upon him, that they muſt undoe him: Never ſo hopefull and ſo ſweet a ſpirit, Misfortune fell ſo foule on. Not yet. When ſhe pleaſe. His love may merit much: his perſon little, For there the match lyes mangled. Ye have pos'd me. She do's, and would doe equall: But will you deale effectually? What ſhall I doe? Of my afflicted heart: ſhe is gon for ever. Ha; ſaiſt thou ſo? nay then thou ſhalt not periſh. O cruell Woman. Excellent Friend. O miracle. Take her withall my heart, thou art ſo honeſt That tis moſt neceſſary I be undone. Be not uncivill Tom, and take your pleaſure. Doe your beſt. HE cannot goe and take no farewell of me, Can he be ſo vnkinde? he's but retir'd Into the Garden or the Orchard: ſee ſirs. Ride, nay then, Had he horſe out? He's gone, My beſtfriends gone Alice? I have loſt the nobleſt,, The trueſt, and the moſt man I ere found yet. He deſerv'd it. Good morrow maſter Michael. Ha? Dreame? I know not, Dreame of a Nunnery? I beare 'em till I breake againe. Good neighbours, no more of it, Ye doe but fling flaxe on my fire: where is ſhe? Farewell, I cannot ſpeake it. Exit Ʋ al. What ſhould I doe friend? But my friend then Whoſe love and loſſe is equall ty'd. O but I forc'd her to it. I will home then, And follow your adviſe, and good, good Michael. Lady, You are met moſt happily: O gentle Doll, You muſt now doe me an eſpeciall favour. I'le tell ye, And let it move you equally: my bleſt Miſtreſſe Vpon a ſlight occaſion taking anger, Tooke alſo (to undoe me) your Aunts Nunnery, From whence by my perſwaſion to redeeme her, Will be impoſſible: nor have I liberty To come, and viſite her: my good, good Dorothy, You are moſt powerfull with her, and your Aunt too, And have acceſſe at all houres liberally, Speake now, or never for me. You will not breake? Good night kinde Miſtreſſe Doll. Exit. Doe not wrong me, I met ye, by my life, juſt as you entred This gentle Ladies Lodge laſt night, thus ſuited About eleven a clocke. I thanke ye. ſqueake within. You have don a friendſhip Worthy the love you beare me. O he's a worthy yong man. My happy Miſtreſſe too: now Fortune helpe me, And all you ſtarres, that governe chaſt deſires Shinne faire, and lovely. As I love my ſoule, Sir. And ſhall do ſtill. Theſe Iewels; I have knowne. Sure, I have knowne theſe Iewels. Good heaven, that they were. And all the worldly bliſſe that heaven can ſend me, And all my prayers and thanks. My beſt friend ſtill: my deereſt: now heaven bleſſe thee And make me worthy of this benefit. Now my beſt Miſtreſſe. And may it proſper, Take her Franciſco: now no more yong Callidon, And love her deerely, for thy father do's ſo. Why how now Miſtreſſe Thomas? Now preſently, and there with nuptiall. The holy Prieſt ſhall make ye happy all.
speeches.Alice: As my womans wit Sir, Which is but weake and crazie. They need not, for beleeve me So well you have manag'd her, and won her minde, Even from her houres of childehood, to this ripeneſſe, And in your abſence, that by me inforced ſtil, So well diſtill'd your gentleneſſe into her, Obſerv'd her, fed her fancy, liv'd ſtill in her, And though Love be a boy, and ever youthfull, And young, and beauteous objects ever aym'd at, Yet here yee have gone beyond love, better'd nature, Made him appeare in yeares, in gray yeares fiery, His bow at full bent ever: feare not brother, For though your body has been farre off from her, Yet every houre your heart, which is your goodneſſe, I have forc'd into her, won a place prepar'd too, And willingly to give it ever harbour: Beleeve ſhe is ſo much yours, and won by miracle, (Which is by age) ſo deep a ſtamp ſet on her By your obſervances, ſhe cannot alter, Were the childe living now ye loſt at ſea Among the Genoway Gallies, what a happineſſe, What a maine bleſſing? 'Tis too true, and too fatall, But peace be with their ſoules. What is he? I obſerve ye, hold your right there, Love and high rule allowes no rivals, brother, He ſhall have faire regard, and all obſervance. Ye have it ſir. Ye are moſt welcome: Ye ſhall find us Happy in our performance. God forgive thee, For againſt thy conſcience thou lyeſt ſtubbornely. 'Tis excellent, And where the outward parts are faire and lovely, (Which are but molds o'th minde) what muſt the ſoule be? Put caſe youth has his ſwinge, and fyery nature Flames to mad uſes many times. I doe not counſell that, ſee him reclaim'd firſt, Which will not prove a miracle, yet Mary I am afraid 'twill vexe thee horribly To ſtay ſo long. What was your dreame to night? for I obſerv'd ye Hugging of me; with good, deere, ſweet Tom. On my word 'tis true wench: And then ye kiſs'd me Mary, more then once too, And ſigh'd, and O ſweet Tom againe: nay, doe not bluſh, Ye have it at the heart wench. And ſo will you too, Or breake down hedges for it: Dorothea, The welcom'ſt woman living: how do's thy brother? I heare he's turn'd a wondrous civill gentleman Since his ſhort travell. Thou wouldſt howle then. O cogging raſcall. Come, do not maske your ſelfe, but ſee him freely, Ye have a minde. A ſhrewd diſſembling queane. Yes, and will not looſe him, Vnleſſe he leap into the Moone, beleeve that, And then ſhee'l ſcramble too: yong wenches loves Are like the courſe of quarterns, they may ſhift And ſeeme to ceaſe ſometimes, and yet we ſee The leaſt diſtemper puls 'em backe againe, And ſeats 'em in their old courſe: feare her not, Vnleſſe he be a devill. Some northerne toy, a little broad. What a mad boy is this? What a letter Has this thing written, how it roares like thunder? With what a ſtate he enters into ſtile. Deere Miſtreſſe. Well, there be waies to reach her yet: ſuch likeneſſe As you two carry me thinkes. Be ſure then His tewgh be tith and ſtrong: and next no ſwearing, He'l catch no fiſh elſe. Farewell Doll. 'Twere good ſome preparation. Some warme broths To purge the bloud, and keep your bed a day Sir, And ſweat it out. Some ſee his bed made. He growes fainter. A purge firſt, And if he breath'd a veyne. He's loth to ſpeake. I doe not like that ſigne. Good Monſieur Thomas, You'r welcome from your travell: I am haſty, A Gentleman lies ſicke ſir. Excellent well, As well as may be, thank ye. I cannot ſtay. I cannot ſtay. My good Monſieur, I have no time to talke now, She will not, I can aſſure you that, and ſo I cannot, nor I will not: good Lord. Ezit. O deere brother, The Gentleman if ev • r you will ſee him Alive as I think. I hope we bring ye health ſir: how is't with ye? Your enemy I ſee has done his worſt. Come, we muſt have ye Luſty againe, and frolicke man; leave thinking You ſhall be well then, And ſuddenly, and ſoundly well. Who's that ſir, Another ſicke man. Doe yo' know the voyce ſir? Now heaven help him. Now I know him. He would not ride there certain, thoſe were planted Onely for walkes I take it. Inded ſir, he deſerves all praiſe. Sure he will returne ſir, He cannot be ſo harſh. He was the worthieſt welcome. Nor wanted, to our knowledge. T'is not her houre of waking. Not to night ſir. Nor any night this weeke elſe. Late yeſter night. No ſir, I left her at her prayers: why doe ye aske me? I know ſhe's there ſir, And all this but a dreame? I will ſatisfie ye, Exit. Not yonder ſir, nor has not this night certaine Bin in her bed. For heaven take leave him not. Alas, he's much afflicted, They are they, certaine. My brother's full of paſſion, I'le ſpeake to him. Now, as you are a gentleman, reſolve me, Where did you get theſe jewels? 'Tis Franciſco brother, By heaven I ty'd 'em on: a little more ſir, A little, little more, what parents have ye? What ſaid that Merchant? Down o' your knees, ſir, For now you have found a father, and that father That will not venture ye againe in Gallyes.
But good Alice Tell me how fares the gentle Cellide, The life of my affection, ſince my travell, My long, and lazie travell? is her love ſtill Vpon the growing hand? do's it not ſtop And wither at my yeares? has ſhe not view'd And entertain'd ſome yonger ſmooth behaviour Some youth but in his bloſſome, as her ſelfe is? There lyes my feares. O no more good ſiſter, Touch no more that ſtring, 'tis too harſh and jarring. With that childe all my hopes went, and you know The root of all thoſe hopes, the mother too Within few dayes. For her loſſe I hope, the beauteous Cellide. Ye are noble, Pray be acquainted with her, keep your way ſir, My coſin and my ſiſter. Come no more complement: cuſtome has made it Dull, old, and tedious: ye are once more welcome, As your owne thoughts can make ye, and the ſame ever. And ſo wee'l in to ratifie it. I lookt for't: Shall we enjoy your companie? We bar all prayers. Exeunt all but Hylas. All that may be: It ſhall be no blinde wedding: and all the joy Of all our friends I hope: he lookes worſe hourely: How do's my friend, my ſelfe? he ſweats too coldly, His pulſe, like the ſlow dropping of a ſpowt, Scarce gives his function: how i'st man, alas ſir, You looke extreme ill: is it any old griefe, The weight of which? I knew the cauſe to be ſo. Come, leade him in, he ſhall to bed: a vomit, I'le have a vomit for him. No, no, no bleeding, A Clyſter will coole all. Away to's chamber, Softly, he's full of paine, be diligent With all the care ye have: would I had ſcus'd him. Exeunt Ye are welcome: Is there no conſtancy in earthly things: No happineſſe in us, but what muſt alter, No life without the heavy load of fortune? What miſeries we are, and to our ſelves, Even then when full content ſeemes to ſit by us, What daily ſores, and ſorrowes? He ſhould be, for he is neere me. Deere Cellide. Why let him dye then. And I my croſſes. Exeunt. Goe to him friend, and comfort him: Ile leade ye: O my beſt joy, my worthieſt friend, ptay pardon me, I am ſo over-joy'd I want expreſſion: I may live to be thankfull: bid your friends welcome. All ſiſter, All, all, and all too little: O that honeſty, That ermine honeſty, unſpotted ever, That perfect goodneſſe. O never, never, Never returne, thou know'ſt not where the cauſe lyes. I will tell thee, Within this houre, things that ſhall ſtartle thee. He never muſt returne. Enter Michael. I thinke ſhe do's. Did ſhe not cry out, 'twas my folly too That forc'd her to this Nunnery? did ſhe not curſe me? For God ſake ſpeake: did you not dreame of me too, How baſely, poorely, tamely, like a foole, Tir'd wi • h his joyes? Say he come backe To piece his poor friends life out? and my miſtreſſe Be vow'd for ever a recluſe? Can ye forget me? Did not you promiſe all your helpe and cunning In my behalfe, but for one houre to ſee her, Did you not ſweare it? by this hand, no ſtrictneſſe Nor rule this houſe holds, ſhall by me, be broken. Nothing but mirth now, friends.
speeches.Hylas: Ye are welcome noble Sir. With all my heart, your leave Lady. A ſhrewd ſmart touch, which do's prognoſticate A body keene and active, ſomewhat old, But that's all one: age brings experience And knowledge to diſpatch. I muſt be better And neerer in my ſervice, with your leave ſir, To this faire Lady.
Yf'aith y'are welcome home; what news beyond ſeas? Still the admirer of their goodneſſe with all my heart now I love a woman of her yeares, a pacer That lay the bridle in her neck will travell Forty, and ſomewhat fulſome is a fine diſh, Theſe yong colts; are too sketiſh. Your faire coſin? I am an aſſe I doe perceive now: a blinde aſſe, a blockhead: For this is handſomneſſe, this that that drawes us, Body and bones: oh what a mounted forehead, What eyes and lips, what every thing about her? How like a Swan ſhe ſwims her pace, and beares Her ſilver breaſts? this is the woman, ſhe, And onely ſhe, that I will ſo much honour As to thinke worthy of my love, all older Idols I heartily abhorre, and give to gunpowder, And all complexions beſides hers, to Gypſies. Harke ye Valentine, Is wild oates yet come over? As mad a worme as ere he was. Ile wayt on ye: Only a thought, or two. This laſt wench, I this laſt wench was a faire one: A dainty wench, a right one: a devill take it, What doe I ayle; to have fifteene now in liking Enough a man would thinke to ſtay my ſtomack, But what's fifteene, or fifteene ſcore to my thoughts? And wherefore are mine eyes made, and have lights, But to encreaſe my objects? this laſt wench Sticks plaguy cloſe unto me: a hundred pound I were as cloſe to her: if I lov'd now As many fooliſh men doe, I ſhould run mad. Don Thomaſio. De bene venew. Thou art not alter'd, They ſaid thou wert all Monſieur. A ſound Convertite. By'r Lady, I have giv'n a ſhrewd puſh at it, for as I take it, The laſt I fell in love with, ſcor'd ſixteene. No ſurely, Nor any wiſe man I thinke; marriage? Would you have me now begin to be prentize, And learne to cobble other mens old boots? Where? can you tell me? Or if 'twere poſſible I might get a Maid, To what uſe ſhould I put her? looke upon her, Dandle her upon my knee, and give her ſuger ſops? All the new gowns i'th pariſh will not pleaſe her, If ſhe be high bred, for ther's the ſport ſhe aymes at, Nor all the feathers in the Fryars. And begin a new order, Live in a dead mans monument, not I ſir, I'le keep mine old road, a true mendicant: What pleaſure this day yeelds me, I never covet To lay up for the morrow: and me thinks ever Another mans cooke dreſſes my dyet neateſt. J have had ſuch damſels J muſt confeſſe. I am looking at her legs, prethee be quiet. A cleane inſtep, And that I love a life: I did not marke This woman halfe ſo well before, how quicke And nimble like a ſhadow, there her leg ſhew'd: By th' mas a neat one, the colour of her ſtocking, A much inviting colour. Pretty breeches, Finely becomming too. Well you ſhall heare more from me. By any meanes. Away then. Exeunt Where are the gentlewomen That ſhould attend him, ther's the patent Me thinks theſe women. He muſt not touch it, 'Tis preſent death. Where are theſe women I ſay? So long, and yet no bolting. Let 'em enter. Or meeting with the ſtygian humour. Forc'd with a cataplaſme of crackers. Scowre all before him, like a Scavenger. I take it ſo, or ſhall be, for ſay the belly-ake Caus'd by an inundation of Peaſe-porridge, Are we therefore to open the port veyne, Or the port Eſquiline? And wilt thou be gone ſaies to'ther? And who elſe? Oh. I would faine Talke with the gentlewomen. To what end? What other end came we along? Come then, Perſwade your ſelfe. Deſpaire not, 'tis not manly: one houres goodneſſe Strikes off an infinite of ils. O rarely well. You ſpoke to me firſt. Your will be done Sir. Who ſhall anſwere this? May we diſcourſe too On honourable tearmes? May we ſing too? For ther's my maſter-piece. But hark ye one word Tom, we may be beaten. She has men enough, My head, my head, Oh my head's kil'd. Away with me for Gods ſake, A Surgeon. A Surgeon. Exit all but Fidler. I Care not for my broken head, But that it ſhould be his plot, and a wench too, A lowzie, lazie wench prepar'd to doe it. I am reſolv'd To call him to account, was it not manifeſt He meant a miſchiefe to me, and laughed at me, When he lay roaring out, his leg was broken, And no ſuch matter: had he broke his necke, Indeed 'twould ne'r ha griev'd me: gallowes gall him, Why ſhould he chooſe out me? Well, if I live, I'le have a new tricke for him. No, no, I will not fight. No upon better thought, I will not fight Sam, But watch my time Yes faith Sam, I love 'em ev'n as well as ev'r I did, Nay, if my braines were beaten out, I muſt to 'em. Any woman Of what degree or calling. Of any age, from fourſcore to fourteen boy, Of any faſhion. Right. For thoſe I love to leade me to repentance: A woman with no noſe, after my ſurquedry, Shewes like King Philips morall, memento mori, And ſhe that has a wodden leg, demonſtrates Like Hypocrites, we halt before the gallowes: An old one with one tooth, ſeemes to ſay to us Sweet meats have ſowre ſawce: ſhe that's full of aches, Crum not your bread before you taſte your porridge, And many morals we may finde. Let's conſider, An houre or two, how I may fit this fellow. That at my danger. Exeunt. Muſick. I Have dog'd his ſiſter, ſure 'twas ſhe, And I hope ſhe will come back again this night too: I Heard the doores clap: now, and't be thy will, wench By th' mas ſhe comes: you are ſurely melt faire gen tlewoman, I take it Miſtris Doll, Sebaſtians daughter. How dare you walk ſo late ſo ſweet: ſo weak guarded? Harke ye. What if a man ſhould kiſſe ye? Her lips are monſtrous rugged, but that ſurely Is but the ſharpneſſe of the weather: harke ye once more, And in your eare, ſweet Miſtreſſe, for ye are ſo, And ever ſhall be from this houre: I have vow'd it. By this white hand Doll. I have no maw to marriage, yet this raſcall Tempts me extreamely: will ye marry preſently? Nothing to night ſweet? You'l follow? Kiſſe. Me thinkes her mouth ſtill Is monſtrous rough, but they have waies to mend it, Farewell. Is there nev'r a ſhop open? I'le give thee a paire of gloves Sam. What do'ſt thou thinke? By th' maſſe but I am, all to be married, I am i'th order now Sam. Ev'n the ſweeteſt woman, The rareſt woman Samuel, and the luſtieſt, But wondrous honeſt, honeſt as the ice boy, Not a bit before hand, for my life, ſirha, And of a luſty kindred. The yong gentleman and I are like to be friends a gaine, The fates will have it ſo. All wrongs forgot. No, ther's the tricke I owe hi • Tis done boy, we are faſt faith, my youth now Shall know I am aforehand, for his qualities. None, but up and ride boy: I have made her no joynture neither, there I have paid him. She ſhall be, as I'le uſe her, And if ſhe anger me, all his abuſes I'le clap upon her Caſſocke. 'Tis paſt that Sam, come, J muſt meet her preſently, And now ſhalt ſee me, a moſt glorious husband. Mas tis ſhe indeed How ſmart the pretty theefe lookes? 'morrow Miſtreſſe. Maids muſt do ſo, at firſt. Yes marry would I A little with your Ladiſhip. Doll, I would have ye preſently prepare your ſelfe And thoſe things you would have with you, For my houſe is ready. And this night not to faile, you muſt come to me, My Friends will all be there too: For Trunks, & thoſe things And houſhold ſtuffe, and clothes you would have carried To morrow, or the next day, ile take order: Onely, What money you have, bring away with ye, And Iewels: I, for adornement There's a bed up, to play the game in, Dorothy, And now come kiſſe me heartily. This Lady ſhalbe welcome too. Your neighbour can reſolve ye. It may be ſo: Come, ye may ſpeake now boldly There's none but friends, Wench. Are not you my Wife? did not I marry you laſt night At St. Michaels Chappell? Are not you Miſtreſſe Dorothy, Thomas ſiſter? S' pretious; you'll make me mad; did not the Prieſt Sir Hugh that you appointed, about twelve a clocke Tye our hands faſt? did not you ſweare you lov'd me? Did not I court ye, comming from this gentlewomans? Be not ſo confident. Is the devill ſtirring? Well, goe with me: for now I wilbe married. Exeunt Nay, I will finde him. Nay then, good morrow, Now J perceive the knavery. Not I, by no meanes. I am very well ſir. No. If you can love me, well. You muſt allow me another Miſtreſſe. Well, let's together then, a luſty kindred.
My coſin Mary In all her joy Sir to congratulate Your faire returne. HEe cannot be ſo wilde ſtill. Grant all that: Is he the firſt, that h'as bin giv'n a loſt man, And yet come fairely home? he is yong, and tender And fit for that impreſſion; your affections Shall ſtamp upon him, age brings on diſcretion, A yeere hence, theſe mad toyes that now poſſeſſe him Will ſhew like bugbeares to him, ſhapes to fright him; Marriage diſſolves all theſe like miſts. 'Tis your feare Which is a wiſe part in you; yet your love However you may ſeeme to leſſen it with theſe diſlikes, and choake it with theſe errors, Do what you can will break out to excuſe him, Ye have him in your hart, and planted, Coſin, From whence the power of reaſon, nor diſcretion Can ever roote him. How willingly thy heart betrayes thee coſin? Cozen thy ſelfe no more: thou haſt no more power To leave off loving him, then he that's thirſty Has to abſtaine from drinke ſtanding before him. His mind is not ſo monſtrous for his ſhape If I have eyes; I have not ſeene his better. A hanſom browne complexion Had I ſaid ſo You would have wiſh'd my tongue out: then his making. A body too, This is for your ſake Mary: take heed coſen, A man is not ſo ſoone made. Weepe truly And with compaſſion Coſin. Foole be with thee. Exit. Ma. and Al.
A thouſand thanks to heaven Sir For your ſafe, voyage, and returne. O 'tis a kiſſe you would ſir, Take it, and tye your tongue up. I told thee what thou hadſt done, miſchiefe go with thee,
speeches.Mary: Thinke not ſo deere Vncle, I left her on her knees, thanking the gods With teares and prayers. She will not belong from ye. If any thing in our poore powers faire ſir To render ye content, and liberall welcome May but appeare, command it. 'Tis ſtrange That nothing can redeeme him: raile him hence, Or ſing him out in's owne way, any thing To be deliver'd of him. What do'ſt thou meane to doe? What haſt thou done? thou haſt broke his neck. Goe run for helpe. Run all, and all too little, O curſed beaſt that hurt him, run, run, flye, He will be dead elſe. Good friend goe you too. Pox o'your Muſicke, Ther's twelve pence for ye.
My joy has ſo much overmaſtered me, That in my teares for your returne. When heaven, and you ſir Shall thinke it fit: for by your wils I am govern'd, I have ſuch cordials, That if you will but promiſe me to take 'em, Indeed you ſhall be well, and very quickly, I'le be your Doctor, you ſhall ſee how finely I'le fetch ye up againe. And thoſe julips in the window. How hard he holds my hand Aunt? O he faints, for heaven ſake, For heaven ſake ſir. My pity thinks ſir, 'Tis great misfortune, that he ſhould thus periſh. That were a cruelty, when care may cure him, Why doe you weep ſo ſir, he may recover? To doe you ſervice. Sure ſhe's hard hearted, That can looke on, and not relent, and deeply At ſuch a miſery: ſhe is not married? Nor neere it? And pray ſir, Do's he deſerve her truely, that ſhe loves ſo? Is he your friend? Will not he dye then? When th'other ſhall recover? 'Tis A hard taske you put me: yet for your ſake I will ſpeake to her: all the art I have: My beſt endevors: all his youth, and perſon, His mind more full of beautis: all his hopes, The memory of ſuch a ſad example, Ill ſpoken of, and never old: the curſes Of loving maids, and what may be alleag'd Ile lay before her: what's her name? I am ready You have ſaid enough ſir, And more then ere I thought that tongue could utter, But ye are a man, a falſe man too. And now, to ſhew you that I am a woman Rob'd of her reſt, and fool'd out of her fondneſſe, The Gentleman ſhall live: and if he love me, Ye ſhall be both my triumphs: I will to him, And as you careleſly fling off your fortune, And now grow weary of my eaſie winning, So will I loſe the name of Valentine, From henceforth all his flatteries, and beleeve it, Since ye have ſo ſo ſlightly parted with affection, And that affection you have pawn'd your faith for: From this houre, no repentance, vowes, nor prayers Shall plucke me backe agen: what I ſhall doe, Yet I will undertake his cure, expect it, Shall miniſter no comfort, no content To either of ye, but hourely more vexations. No, ſo much I have loved To be commanded by you, that even now, Even in my hate I will obey your wiſhes. Dye like a foole unſorrow'd? A bankrupt foole, that flings away his treaſure? I muſt begin my cure. Take your deſire ſir, And in a nobler way, for I dare truſt ye, No other fruit my love muſt ever yeeld yee, I feare no more: yet your moſt conſtant memory (So much I am wedded to that worthineſſe) Shall ever be my friend, companion, husband, Farewell, and fairely governe your affections, Stand, and deceive me not: O noble yong man, I love thee with my ſoule, but dare not ſay it: Once more farewell, and proſper. Exit. No vertuous mother, Tis for my holy health, to purchaſe which They ſhall forget the childe of eaſe, ſoft ſlumbers, O my afflicted heart, how thou art tortur'd, And Love, how like a tyrant, thou raign'ſt in me, Commanding and forbidding at one inſtant: Why came I hither that deſire to have Onely all liberty, to make me happy? Why didſt thou bring that yong man home, O Ʋ alentine, That vertuous youth, why didſt thou ſpeake his goodneſſe In ſuch a phraſe, as if all tongues, all praiſes Were made for him? O fond and ignorant, Why didſt thou foſter my affection Till it grew up, to know no other father, And then betray it? Yes, Mother, My ſorrowes onely. What make ye here? Now ſir, I come to ye. Not for the world, now, Mother, And thus ſir, all my ſerviee I pay to you, And all my love to him.
Ye are too munificent, Nor am I able to conceive thoſe thanks ſir. It is a jewell I doe confeſſe would make a thiefe, but never Of him that's ſo much yours, and bound your ſervant, That were a baſe ingratitude. I doe Tom. What, new worke? All this forc'd foolery will never doe it.
The poore ſervant Of both your goodneſſes preſents his ſervice. None, gentle ſir, that I feele Your love is too too tender. Nay beleeve ſir, 'Tis a joy to be ill, Where ſuch a vertuous faire Phyſitian Is ready to releeve: your noble cares I muſt, and ever ſhall be thankfull for, And would my ſervice (I dare not looke upon her) But be not fearefull, I feele nothing dangerous, A grudging caus'd by th' alteration Of ayre, may hang upon me: my heart's whole, (I would it were) No, you ſhall never know it. How that touch ſtung me? Not by thouſands: Now what 'tis to be truely miſerable, I feele at full experience. Good Gentlemen, Good learned Gentlemen. Pray leave me: I beſeech ye leave me gentlemen. I have no other ſickneſſe but your preſence, Convey your Cataplaſmes to thoſe that need 'em, Your Vomits, and your Clyſters. Till doomeſ-day: what unneceſſary nothings Are theſe about a wounded minde? What queſtions they propound too: how do you ſir? I am glad to ſee you well. And can you tell me How old I am then? there's my hand, pray ſhew me How many broken ſhins within this two yeare. Who would be thus in fetters, good maſter Doctor, And you deere Doctor, and the third ſweet Doctor And pretious maſter Apothecary, I doe pray ye To give me leave to live a little longer, Ye ſtand before me like my blacks. Would you were all rotten That ye might only intend one anothers itches: Or would the Gentlemen with one conſent Would drinke ſmall Beere but ſeven yeare, and aboliſh That wildfire of the bloud, unſatiate wenching That your too Indies, ſprings and fals might faile ye What torments theſe intruders into bodies. Bleſſe me, what beames Flew from theſe angell eyes: O what a miſery What a moſt ſtuddied torment tis to me now To be an honeſt man: dare ye ſit by me? You are a faire Phyſitian: You bring no bitterneſſe gilt ore, to gull us No danger in your lookes, yet there my death lyes. Of which Lady? Sure ſhe has found my griefe? why do you bluſh ſo? What heaven ye have brought me Lady? A vertuous bleſſing crowne ye O goodly ſweet, can there be ſo much charity So noble a compaſſion in that heart That's filled up with anothers faire affections? Can mercy drop from thoſe eyes. Can miracles be wrought upon a dead man, When all the power ye have, and perfect object Lyes in anothers light: and his deſerves it? Hold for heaven ſake, Muſt my friends miſery make me a triumph? Beare I that noble name, to be a Traitor? O vertuous goodnes, keepe thy ſelfe untainted: You have no power to yeeld, nor he to render Nor I to take: I am reſolv'd to die firſt. And though I love ye above the light ſhines on me, Beyond the wealth of Kingdomes, free content, Sooner would ſnatch at ſuch a bleſſing offer'd Then at my pardon'd life by the law forfeited, Yet, yet O noble beauty, yet O paradiſe For you are all the wonder reveal'd of it, Yet is a gratitude to be preſerv'd A worthy gratitude to one moſt worthy. The name, and noblenes of friends. Do you make a doubt? For vertues ſake take heed. This cannot be. Pray ſtay there: Me thinks you are not faire now; me thinks more That modeſt, vertue, men delivered of you Shewes but like ſhadow to me, thin, and fading. Ye have no ſhare in goodneſſe: Ye are belyde; you are not Cellide, The modeſt, unaculate: who are ye? For I will know: what devill to do miſchiefe Vnto my vertuous Friend, hath ſhifted ſhapes With that unblemiſhed beauty. O double hearted, O woman, perfect woman: what diſtraction Was meant to mankind when thou was't made a devill, What an invyting hell invented? tell me, And if you yet remember what i • goodneſſe, Tell me by that, and truth, can one ſo cheriſh'd So ſainted in the ſoule of him, whoſe ſervice Is almoſt turn'd to ſupperſtition, Whoſe every day endeavours, and deſires Offer themſelves like incenſe on your altar, Whoſe heart holds no int • lligence, but holy And moſt religious with his love; whoſe life (And let it ever be remembred Lady) Is drawne out only for your ends. Whoſe all, and every part of man: pray make me Like ready Pages wait upon y • ur pleaſures; Whoſe breath is but your bubble. Can ye, dare ye, Muſt ye caſt of this man, though he were willing, Though in a noblenes, ſo croſſe my danger His friendſhip durſt confirme it, without baſeneſſe, Without the ſtaine of honour? ſhall not people Say liberally hereafter, ther's the Lady That loſt her Father, Friend, herſelfe, her faith too, To fawne upon a ſtranger, for ought you know As faithleſſe as your ſelfe, in love as fruitleſſe? Good heaven, what is this woman? Whether doe you drive me? Is this ſerious? How like the Sun Labouring in his eclipſe, darke, and prodigious, She ſhew'd till now? when having won her way, How full of wonder he breakes out againe, And ſheds his vertuous beames: excellent Angell, For no leſſe can that heavenly minde proclaime thee, Honour of all thy ſexe, let it be lawfull, And like a pilgrim thus I kneele to beg it, Not with prophane lips now, nor burnt affections, But, reconcil'd to faith, with holy wiſhes, To kiſſe that virgin hand. Goodneſſe guide thee: My wonder like to fearefull ſhapes in dreames, Has wakened me out of my fit of folly, But not to ſhake it off: a ſpell dwels in me, A hidden charme ſhot from this beauteous woman, That fate can ne'r avoid, nor phyſicke finde, And by her counſell ſtrengthen'd: onely this Is all the helpe I have, I love faire vertue. Well, ſomething I muſt doe, to be a friend, Yet I am poore, and tardy: ſomething for her too, Though I can never reach her excellence, Yet but to give an offer at a greatneſſe. I am o'th mending hand. Thou art a mad companion: never ſtaid Tom? What haſt thou there, a julip? What? I ſee no harme Tom, Drinke with a moderation. Sir, I much thanke ye, And ſhall be carefull: yet a glaſſe or two So fit I finde my body, and that ſo needfull. Doe, I'le pledge thee. Now or never gentlemen, Doe me a kindeneſſe and deliver me. From theſe things, that talke within there, Phyſitians, Tom, Phyſitians, ſcowring-ſticks, They meane to reade upon me. My learned Tom. Pray ye thanke 'em, And tell 'em my moſt ſickneſſe is their abſence: Ye ſee my company. My beſt viſitants, I ſhall be govern'd by ye. What a ſtrange fellow's this? Yes, 'tis a gentlemans that's much afflicted In's minde: great pitty Ladies. He came to me, to aske free pardon of me, For ſome things done long ſince, which his diſtemper Made to appeare like wrong, but 'twas not ſo. How exactly This cunning yong theefe plaies his part. O ye grand Aſſe. Gon; ſhe found you out, and finely, In your own nooze ſhe halter'd ye: you muſt be whiſpering To know how things ſhowd: not content to fare well But you muſt roare out roſt meate; till that ſuſpition You carried it moſt neately, ſhe beleeved too And wept moſt tenderly; had you continew'd, Without doubt you had brought her off. Good night, tis almoſt bed time: yet no ſleepe Muſt enter theſe eyes, till I worke a wonder. Exit. A boat, a boat, a boat. Whether are ye bound friends? May I have paſſage for my money? Then merrily aboard, and noble friend Heauens goodneſſe keep thee ever, and all vertue Dwell in thy boſome Cellide, my laſt teares J leave behinde me thus, a ſacrifice, For I dare ſtay no longer to betray ye. Fellow? I doe obey ye: But I beſeech ye ſir, informe me truely How I am guilty. It ſhall be ſo, and here I'le end all miſeries, Since friendſhip is ſo cruell, I confeſſe it, And which is more, a hundred of theſe robberies: This Ring I ſtole too from him: and this jewell The firſt and laſt of all my wealth: forgive me My innocence and truth, for ſaying I ſtole 'em, And may they prove of value but to recompence The thouſand part of his love, and bread I have eaten. Pray ſee 'em render'd noble ſir, and ſo I yeeld me to your power. How you pleaſe ſir, I am reſolv'd, nor can a joy or miſery Much move me now. Faith ſir, my reſt is up, And what I now pull, ſhall no more afflict me Then if I plaid at ſpan-counter, nor is my face The map of any thing I ſeeme to ſuffer, Lighter affections ſeldome dwell in me ſir. Yes: O my Fortune. Now I'le tell ye, Becauſe blinde fortune yet may make me happy, Of whom I had 'em, I have never heard yet, But from my infancy, upon this arme I ever wore'em. None That J know yet: the more my ſtubborne fortune, But as J heard a Merchant ſay that bred me, Who, to my more affliction, di'de a poore man, When J reach'd eighteen yeers. He ſaid, an infant, in the Genoway Galleyes. But from what place he never could direct me. I was taken in a ſea-fight, and from a Marriner, Out of his manly pitty he redeem'd me. He told me of a Nurſe that waited on me, But ſhe, poore ſoule, he ſaid was killed. A letter too, I had enclos'd within me, To one Caſtructio a Venetian Merchant, To bring me up: the man, when yeers allow'd me, And want of friends compell'd, I ſought, but found him Long dead before, and all my hopes gone with him. The wars was my retreat then, and my travell In which I found this gentlemans free bounty, For which, heaven recompenc'd him: now ye have all. May all hate ſeek me elſe, and thus I ſeale it.
How do's he beare himſelf? I ſhould be glad on't Sir. They are grounded Hereditary in him, from his father And to his grave they will haunt him. Planted in my heart Aunt? Beleeve it no, I never was ſo liberall: What though he ſhew a ſo ſo comely fellow Which we call pretty? or ſay it may be hanſom? What though his promiſes may ſtumble at The power of goodneſſe in him, ſometimes uſe too? Reaſonable Inclining to a tawney. Which may be mended: I have ſeene leggs ſtraiter. And cleaner made. Far neater, And better ſet together. I grant 'tis neat enough. All this You onely uſe, to make me ſay I love him: I doe confeſſe I doe, but that my fondneſſe Should fling it ſelfe upon his deſperate follies. No, no Aunt, no beleeve me. Fye Aunt, Vpon my conſcience. I'le be hang'd firſt, But you muſt have your way. Enter Dorothea. How doe ye friend, I have a quarrell to ye, Ye ſtole away, and left my company. Prethee how is he? thou ſpeakſt truth. Never: ha's forgot me, I heare wench, and his hot love too: And I am glad it ſhould be ſo; his travels Have yeelded him variety of Miſtreſſes, Fairer in his eye farre. I was a foole, but better thoughts I thank heaven. See me friend? doe you thinke it fit? His ſo much contrary To my deſires, ſuch an antipathy That I muſt ſooner ſee my grave. I grant it, For then I daily hop'd his faire converſion. That minde I'le maſter then. Not to his perſon, But to his qualities, his mad-cap follies, Which ſtill like Hydras heads grow thicker on him. I have a credit friend, and maids of my ſort, Love where their modeſties may live untainted. From him? Have ye ſeene it friend? For your ſake, Not that I any way ſhall like his ſcribling. Now heaven bleſſe me. Out, out upon him. Worſe, worſe, and worſe ſtill, Still fowler? Hay, hay boyes: goodneſſe keep me: oh: Here, take your ſpell againe, it burnes my fingers. Was ever Lover writ ſo ſweet a Letter, So elegant a ſtile? pray looke upon't: The rareſt inventory of ranke oathes That ever cut-purſe caſt. Onely i'th bottome A little julip gently ſprinckled over To coole his mouth, leſt it breake out in bliſters, Indeed law. Yours for ever. You ſhall be welcome to me, eome when you pleaſe, And ever may command me vertuouſly, But for your brother, you muſt pardon me, Till I am of his nature, no acceſſe friend, No word of viſitation, as ye love me, And ſo for now Ile leave ye. Exit. VVHen comes he? Then get you up Doll, Away, I'le ſtrait come to you: is all ready? You need no more inſtruction? Speake ſoftly, He is, and there he goes. How he itches? I have found it, Your brothor Thomas, Doll. Pray heavens he be not teaſing. There he ſpeakes ſence, but ile aſſure ye gentleman, I think no Wife of yours: at what houre was it? He's a good handſome fellow, Play not the foole.
SIrha, no more of your French ſhrugs J adviſe you, If you be lowzie, ſhift your ſelfe. I ſay to 'th purpoſe. Sirha, do not conjure me with your French furies. Che doga vou, Raſcall: Leave me your rotten language, and tell me plainely And quickly ſirha, left I crack your French crowne, What your good Maſter meanes: I have maintain'd You and your Monſieur, as I take it Launcelot Theſe two yeeres at your ditty vous, your jours: Jour me no more, for not another penny Shall paſſe my purſe. What Tom, boy, welcome with all my heart boy, Welcome 'faith, thou haſt gladded me at ſoule boy, Infinite glad I am, I have praied too, Thomas For you wilde Thomas, Tom, I thank thee hartily For comming home. How's this? Humh, humh, Diſcretion? is it come to that? the boy's ſpoild. A pox o' travell, I ſay. Prethee no more; t'is ſcurvy; ther's thy ſiſter Vndon without redemption: he eates with picks Vtterly ſpoyld, his ſpirit baffell'd in him. How have I find that this affliction Should light ſo heavie on me. I have no more ſonnes; And this no more mine owne, no ſpark of nature Allows him mine now, he's growne tame: my grand curſe Hang ore his head that thus transform'd thee: travell? Ile ſend my horſe to travell next: we monſieur, Now will my moſt canonicall deere neighbours Say I have found my ſonne, and rejoyce with me Becauſe he has mew'd his mad tricks off. I know not, But I am ſure; this Monſieur, this fine gentleman Will never be in my books like mad Thomas, I muſt goe ſeeke an heire, for my inheritance Muſt not turne ſecretary: my name and quality Has kept my land three hundred yeers in madneſſe, And it ſlip now, may it ſinke. Exit. Sirha, I ſay ſtill you have ſpoild your Maſter: leave your ſtiches: I ſay thou haſt ſpoild thy maſter. Marry thou haſt taught him like an arrant raſcall, Firſt to reade perfectly: which on my bleſſing I warn'd him from: for I knew if he read once, He was a loſt man. Secondly, ſir Launcelot, Sir lowſie Launcelot, ye have ſuffer'd him Againſt my power firſt, then againſt my precept, To keepe that ſimpring ſort of people company, That ſober men call civill: marke ye that Sir? It does not pleaſe my worſhip, Nor ſhall not pleaſe my worſhip: third and laſtly, Which if the law were here, I would hang thee for, (However I will lame thee) like a villaine, Thou haſt wrought him Cleane to forget what 'tis to doe a miſchiefe, A handſome miſchiefe, ſuch as thou knew'ſt I lov'd well. My ſervants all are ſound now, my drink ſowrd, Not a horſe pawnd, nor plaid away: no warrants Come for the breach of peace. Men travell with their money, and nothing meets 'em: I was accurs'd to ſend thee, thou wert ever Leaning to lazineſſe, and loſſe of ſpirit, Thou ſlept'ſt ſtill like a corke upon the water, Your worſhip knowes, I ever was accounted The moſt deboſh'd, and pleaſe you to remember, Every day drunke too, for your worſhips credit, I broke the Butlers head too. No baſe Palliard J doe remember yet that anſlaight, thou waſt beaten, And fledſt before the Butler: a blacke jacke Playing vpon thee furiouſly, J ſaw it: I ſaw thee ſcatter'd rogue, behold thy Maſter. Tom, when is the horſe-race? You will be there? Spoild for ever, The cocking holds at Derby, and there will be Iacke Wild-oats, and Will Purſer. Yes, I will marry agen: but Monſieur Thomas, What ſay ye to the gentleman that challenged ye Before he went, and the fellow ye fell out with? Any woman: I care not of what colour, or complexion, Any that can beare children: reſt ye merry. Exit. NEver perſwade me, I will marry againe What ſhould I leave my ſtate to, pins & poaking ſticks To Farthingals, and frownces, to fore-horſes And a old leather bawdy houſe behind'en To thee? Where, what is he? Who is he like? Thou lyeſt, thou haſt mard him, Thou, and thy praier bookes: I do diſclaime him: Did not I take him ſinging yeſternight A godly Ballad, to a godly tune too, And had a catechizme in's pocket Damſell, One of your deare diſciples, I perceive it? When did he ride abroad ſince he came over? What Taverne h • s he us'd to? what hings done That ſhewes a man, and mettle? when was my houſe At ſuch a ſhame before, to creep to bed At ten a clocke, and twelve, for want of company? No ſinging, nor no dauncing, nor no drinking? Thou think'ſt not of theſe ſcandals; when, and where Has he but ſhewd his ſword of late. Would thou wert aſhes On that condition; but beleeve it goſſip You ſhall know you have wrong. He is loſt, and ſpoil'd I am reſolv'd my rooffe Shall never harbour him: and for your Minion Ile keepe you cloſe enough, leaſt you breake looſe And do more michiefe; get ye in: who waits. Exit. Dor. Seeke the Boy: and bid him wait My pleaſure in the morning: marke what houſe He is in, and what he do's: and truly tell me. If ye do, ile hang ye. Exeunt. AT Valentines houſe ſo merry? So gameſon doſt thou ſay? Ballads, and Fidles too? Did he do deviſes? Come ſir, what can you ſay? is there any hope yet You Maſter may returne? Is he the old Tom? Goe forward. Handle me that. Good, good. Good ſtill. y'faith a fine Boy. Excellent good ſtill. There eate, and grow againe, I am pleas'd. If this be true, thou little tyny page This tale that thou tell'ſt me Then on thy backe will I preſently hang A handſon new Levery: But if this be falſe, thou little tyney page As falſe it well may be Then with a cudgell of foure foote long Ile beate thee from head to toe. Enter Servant. Will the boy come. Time tries all ther. To be ſhort Thomas Becauſe I feele a ſcruple in my conſcience Concerning the demeanour, and a maine one And therefore like a Father would be ſatisfi'd, Get up to that window there, and preſently Like a moſt compleat Gentleman, come from Tripoly. You Rogue Launcelet, You lying raſcall. Sirha, ſirha. Lancelot du Lake Get you upon adventers: caſt your coate And make your exit. And you too preſently. Bid my maid ſervant come: and bring my daughter I will have one ſhall pleaſe me. Exit ſer. Bring me the money there: here M. Thomas, I pray ſit downe, ye are no more my ſonne now, Good gentleman be cover'd This money I do give ye, becauſe of whilom You have bin thought my ſonne, and by myſelfe too, And ſome things done like me: ye are now another There is two hundred pound, a civill ſome For a yong civill man: much land and Lordſhip Will as I take it now, but prove temptation To dread ye from your ſetled, and ſweet carriage. Nay I beſeech ye cover. It ſhall, to my uſe To mine againe: do you ſee ſir: good fine gentleman, I give no brooding money for a Scrivener, Mine is for preſent trafficke, and ſo ile uſe it. For the maine cauſe Mounſieur I ſent to treat with you about, behold it; Behold that peice of ſtory worke, and view it I want a right heire to inherir me, Not my eſtate alone, but my conditions, From which you are revolted, therefore dead, And I will breake my backe, but I will get one. There, among thoſe Damſels, In mine owne tribe: I know their quallities Which cannot faile to pleaſe me: for their beauties A matter of a three farthings, makes all perfect, A little beere, and beeffe broth: they are ſound too. Stand all a breaſt: now gentle M. Thomas Before I chooſe, you having liv'd long with me, And happely ſometimes with ſome of theſe too, Which fault I never frown'd upon: pray ſhew me (For feare we confound our Genealogies) Which have you laid aboord? ſpeake your mind freely Have you had copulation with that Damſell? Stand you a ſide then: how with her ſir? Retyre you too: ſpeake forward M. Thomas. With all that's ſomewhat large. With all Thomas. A ſigne thou art mine owne yet, In againe all: and to your ſeverall functions. Exit. Maides. What ſay you to yong Luce, my neighbours daughter, She was too yong I take it, when you travelled; Some twelve yeare old? A pretty anſwere, to cut of long diſcourſe, For I have many yet to aske ye of, Where I can chooſe, and nobly, hold up your finger When ye are right: what ſay ye to Valeria; Whoſe husband lies a dying now? why two, And in that forme? A witty morall: have at ye once more Thomas, The ſiſters of St. Albones, all five; dat boy, Dat's mine owne boy. There needes none man: A ſtraw on pardon: prethee need no pardon: Ile aske no more, nor thinke no more of marriage, For O my conſcience I ſhalbe thy Cuckold: Ther's ſome good yet left in him: beare your ſelfe well, You may recover me, ther's twenty pound ſir, I ſee ſome ſparkles which may flame againe, You may eat with me when you pleaſe, you know me. What, are you growne ſo corne ſed gooddy You will not know your Father: what vaga'res Have you in hand, what out leapes, durty heeles That at theſ • houres of night ye muſt be gadding, And through the Orchard take your private paſſage; What, is the breeze in your breech, or has your brother Appointed you an houre of meditation How to demeane himſelfe: get ye to bed, drab Or ile ſo crab your ſhoulders: ye demure ſlut Ye civill diſh of ſliced beefe get ye in. Is't ev'n ſo Dame Have at ye with a night ſpell then. St. Geoge, St. George, our Ladies knight He walkes by day, ſo do's he by night, And when he had her found He her beat, and her bound, Vntill to him her troth ſhe plight, She would not ſtir from him that night. Vp with your noſe ſir, I doe not bleed, 'twas a ſound knock ſhe gave me, A plaguy mankinde gi • le, how my braines totters? Well, go thy waies, thou haſt got one thouſand pound more With this dog tricke, Mine owne true ſpirit in her too, Who wouldſt thou make me beleeve it was, the divell? He? if it be ſo, I'le put thee in my Will, and ther's an end on't. No more words then, we'l watch him: thou'lt not beleeve Lance, How heartily glad I am. No more words, but watch him. Exeunt. Why that's my daughter, rogue, do'ſt thou not ſee her Kiſſing that fellow there, there in that corner? Now, now, now they agree o'th match too. Hang Boots ſir, Why they'l weare breeches too. Why now they kiſſe againe, there I knew 'twas ſhe, and that her crafty ſtealing Out the back way muſt needs have ſuch a meaning. Why do'ſt thou follow me? Thou raſcall ſlave haſt thou not twice abus'd me? Haſt thou not ſpoil'd the boy? by thine owne covenant, Would'ſt thou not now be hang'd? Thou ſayeſt right Lance, And ther's my hand once more. Didſt thou heare that? And he ſhall marry her, for it ſeems ſhe likes him, And their firſt boy ſhall be my heire. Come, follow cloſe, I'le ſee the end ſhe aymes at, And if he be a handſome fellow Launcelot, • iat, 'tis done, and all my ſtate is ſetled. Exeunt. Peace, let my joy worke eaſely Ha, boy: art there my boy: mine owne boy, Tom. boy, Home Lance, and ſtrike a freſh peece, of wine, the townes ours, A notable brave boy. I'le give thee five hundred pound more for that word. I'le bar that firſt. Ther's all boy, The keyes of all I have, come, let's be merry, For now I ſee thou art right.
May it pleaſe your worſhip: Then to anſwer punctually. Then J ſay to'th purpoſe, Becauſe your Worſhips vulgar underſtanding May meet me at the neereſt: your ſonne, my maſter, Or Monſieur Thomas, (for ſo his travell ſtiles him) Through many forraigne plots that vertue meets with, And dangers ( I beſeech ye give attention) Is at the laſt ariv'd To aske your (as the French man cals it ſweetly) Benediction, ae jour en jour. Che ditt'a vou, Monſieur. Your Worſhip is erroneous, For as I told you, your Sonne Tom, or Thomas, My Maſter, and your ſonne is now arriv'd To aske ye, as our language beares it neereſt Your quotidian bleſſing, and here he is in perſon. Sir, as J ſpeake eight languages, I onely Told him you came to aske his benediction, De jour enjour. I ſay how ſir? And't pleaſe your worſhip. I have him here, a rare rogue, good ſweet maſter, Doe ſomething of ſome ſavour ſuddenly, That we may eat, and live: I am almoſt ſtarv'd, No point manieur, no point devein, no Signieur, Not by the vertue of my languages, Nothing at my old maſters to be hoped for, O Signieur du, nothing to line my life with, But cold Pyes with a cudgell, till you help us. I heare no ſtirring any where, no light In any window, 'tis a night for the nonce Sir. O damſell deere, Open the doore, and it ſhall appeare, Open the doore, O gentle ſquire. Vp, up, I warrant ye. Be patient ſir, be patient: let me binde it. He went far elſe I will aſſure your worſhip on my credit By the faith of a Travellor, and a Gentleman, Your ſonne in found againe, the ſonne, the Tom. The old Tom. Next, to conſider how he is the old Tom. I would ye had ſeene it handled Laſt night ſir, as we handled it: cap à pe, Footte for leers, and learings; O the noyſe The noyſe we made. The windowes clattring And all the Chambermaides, in ſuch a whobub, One with her ſmocke halfe off; another in haſt Wi • h a ſerving mans hoſe upon her head. A fellow rayling out of a loop hole there And his mouth ſtopt with durt. Here one of our heads broke. The gentleman himſelfe yong M. Thomas, Invirond with his furious Mermidons The fiery Fidler, and my ſelfe; now ſinging, Now beating at the doore, there parlying, Courting at that window, at the other ſcalling And all theſe ſeverall noyſes to two Trenchers, Strung with a bottome of browne thred, which ſhowd ad mirable. Nor here ſir. Gave we the frolicke over: though at length We quit the Ladies Skonce on compoſition But to the ſilent ſtreetes we turn'd our furies: A fleeping watchman here we ſtole the ſhooes from, There made a noyſe, at which he wakes, and followes: The ſtreetes are durty, takes a queene hith cold, Hard cheeſe, and that choakes him o' Munday next: Windowes, and ſignes we ſent to Erebus; A crue of bawling curs we entertain'd laſt, When having let the pigs looſe in out pariſhes, O the brave cry we made as high as Algate! Downe comes a Conſtable, and the Sow his Siſter Moſt trayterouſly tramples upon Authority, There a whole ſtand of rug gownes rowted manly And the Kings peace put flight: a purblind pig here Runs me his head into the Admirable Lanthorne, Out goes the light, and all turnes to confuſion: A Potter riſes, to enquire this paſſion A Boare imboſt takes ſanctuary in his ſhop. When twenty dogs ruſh after, we ſtill cheering Down goes the pots, and pipkins, down the pudding pans, The creame bols cry revenge here, there the candleſticks. Here he comes now himſelfe ſir. Will ye ſpoile all agen ſir. Why, what a devill do you meane? Let me never eate againe ſir, Nor feele the bleſſing of another blew-coate If this yong Gentleman, ſweet Maſter Thomas Be not as mad as heart can wiſh: your heart ſir, If yeſternights diſcourſe: ſpeake fellow Robin And if thou ſpeakeſt leſſe then truth. O deu guin Can ye deny, ye beat a Conſtable Laſt night. Good M. Thomas. We meane not Thoſe civill things you did at M. Valentines The Fidle, and the fa'las, Pur la mour de dieu Pur me no purs: but pur at that doore, out ſirha Ile beate ye purblind elſe, out ye eight languages, My bloud upon your head. Exit. Lan. Bleſſe my Maſter: looke up ſir I beſeech ye, Vp with your eyes to heaven. In her, alas ſir, Alas poore gentlewoman, ſhe a hand ſo heavy To knocke ye like a Calfe down, or ſo brave a courage To beat her father? if you could beleeve ſir. One that ſpits fire as faſt as he ſometimes ſir, And changes ſhapes as often: your ſonne Thomas: Never wonder, if it be not he, ſtraight hang me. J ſaw his legs, has Boots on like a Player, Vnder his wenches cloaths: 'tis he, 'tis Thomas In his own ſiſters cloaths, ſir, and I can waſt him. May ye be gladder, But not this way ſir. Kiſſing? Why ther's the Boots ſtill ſir. I am at my ſmall wits end. Did ſhe nev'r beat ye before ſir? I thinke I would ſir, But you are ſo impatient: do's not this ſhew ſir, (I do beſeech ye ſpeake, and ſpeake with judgement, And let the caſe be equally conſidered) Far braver in your daughter? in a ſon now 'Tis nothing, of no marke: every man do's it, But, to beget a daughter, a man maiden That reaches at theſe high exploits, is admirable: Nay ſhe goes far beyond him: for when durſt he, But when he was drunke, doe any thing to ſpeake of? This is Sebaſtian truely. I thinke ſhe ſpoke of marriage, I marry Now ye goe right to worke. Do you ſee now plaine? that's Miſtris Dorothy, And that's his Miſtris.
speeches.Seb: Onely to ſee my ſonne, my ſonne good Launcelot Your Maſter, and my ſonne: body O me ſir, No money, no more money Monſieur Launcelot, Not a deneere, ſweet Signior: bring the perſon, The perſon of my boy, my boy Tom: Monſieur Thomas, Or get you gone agen, du gata whee ſir, Baſſa mi cu, good Launcelot, valetote. My boy, or nothing.
Sir, I doe finde your prayers Have much much prevail'd above my ſins. Elſe certaine I had periſh'd with my rudeneſſe, Ere J had won my ſelfe to that diſcretion I hope you ſhall hereafter finde. Sirah, you rogue, look for't, for I will make thee Ten times more miſerable then thou thoughtſt thy ſelfe Before thou travelledſt: thou haſt told my father I know it, and I finde it, all my rogueries By meere way of prevention to undoe me. But that I muſt be civill, I would beat thee like a dog: ſir, howſoever The time I have miſpent may make you doubtfull, Nay, harden your beliefe 'gainſt my converſion, Yet deere father Your owne experience in my after courſes. He did ill in it As he dos all: for I was uttering A handſome ſpeech or two, I have been ſtudying Ere ſince I came from Paris: how glad to ſee thee? Ir ſhallbe ſiſter, For I can doe it when I liſt: a • d yet wench Be mad too when I pleaſe: I have the trick on't. Beware a traveller. Not for the world: but wher's my Miſtreſſe And prethee ſay how do's ſhe? I melt to ſee her, And preſently: I muſt a way. Not ſee me? I'le. No more of that ſweet Doll, I will be civill. Wouldſt thou have me loſe my birth-right? For yond old thing will diſinherit me If I grow too demure: good ſweet Doll, prethee: Prethee deere ſiſter, let me ſee her. Nay, I beſeech thee: by this light. Kiſſe me, and be my friend, we two were twins. And ſhall we now grow ſtrangers? Well, there be other women, and remember You, you were the cauſe of this: there be more lands too, And better people in 'em: fare ye well, And other loves: what ſhall become of me And of my vanities, becauſe they grieve ye. He lyes, that ſayes I doe not. If you pleaſe: for it muſt be ſo. Yes. She is a woman: But he ſhe entertaines next for a ſervant, I ſhall be bold to quarter. Your patience, May not a man profeſſe his Love? Out, out upon thee. how would you have me write? Begin with my love premiſed? ſurely, And by my truly Miſtreſſe What ſweet content dwels here? O good Sir, Remember not thoſe follies: where I have wronged ſir, (So much I have now learn'd to diſcern my ſelfe) My meanes, and my repentance ſhall make even, Nor doe I thinke it any imputation To let the law p • rſwade me. Eight languages, And wither at an old mans words? Then take a widow, A good ſtanch wench, that tith, Thou waſt wont to love old women, fat, and flat noſed, And thou wouldſt ſay they kiſt like Flounders, flat All the face over. I am glad on't, And prethee harke. A while Alice. O ſweete Alice. By heaven. Wee'll goe viſite 'Tis charity: beſides I know ſhe is there: And under viſitation I ſhall ſee hir Will ye along? Be ſure then I be a civill man: J have ſport in hand boyes Shall make mirth for a marriage day. Doe you think I am mad? you'l give me leave To try her fairely? Why there boy, But wher's the ſicke man? Thou thinkſt nothing elſe. How do'ſt thou Frank? how do'ſt thou boy, beare up man: What, ſhrink i'th ſinewes for a little ſickneſſe? Deavolo morte. How like a Flute thou ſpeak'ſt: o'th mending hand man Gogs bores, I am well, ſpeake like a man of worſhip. With theſe eyes friends, my eyes muſt nev'r ſee more. Art not thou man enough too? Thou haſt fleſh enough about thee: if all that maſſe Will not maintaine a little ſpirit, hang it, And dry it too for dogs meat: get you gone; I have things of moment in my minde: that doore, Keep it as thou would'ſt keep thy wife from a Servingman. No more I ſay: away Sam. O what is that to you my foole? O what is that to you, Plucke in your face you bawling Aſſe, Or I will breake your brow. hey down, down, a down. A new Ballad, a new, a new. And art thou ſtrong enough? I ſhall ſtand neerer Ere I be twelve houres older: ther's my buſineſſe, She is monſtrous ſubtile Doll. By this light Doll, Nothing but in the way of honeſty. If ye meane honourably. Fye, fye ſir, Now I have promis'd ye this night to marry, Would ye be ſo intemperate? are ye a gentleman?
Excellent ſiſter, I am glad to ſee thee well: but wher's my father? Ile waſh my hands of all ye do: farewell Sir. Thou art not mad? What bobd of all ſides? Why Doll, why Doll I ſay: my letter ſubd too, And no acceſſe without I mend my manners? All my deſignes in Limbo? I will have her, Yes, I will have her, though the divell rore, I am reſolv'd that, if ſhe live above ground, I'le not be bobd i'th noſe with every bobtaile: I will be civill too: now I thinke better, Exceeding civill, wondrous finely carried: And yet be mad upon occaſion, And ſtarke mad too, and ſave my land: my father: I'le have my will of him, how ere my wench goes. Exit. I know not ſir. Not I ſir, I have forgot thoſe journeyes. I am ſorry ſir, They ſhould employ their time ſo ſlenderly, Their underſtandings will beare better courſes. I'le breake it yet. Goe for a Fidler then: the poore old Fidler That ſayes his ſongs: but firſt where lyes my Miſtreſſe, Did ye enquire out that? 'Tis the happier: Away then, finde this Fidler, and doe not miſſe me By nine a clocke. My father's mad now, And ten to one will diſinherite me: I'le put him to his plunge, and yet be merry, What Rybabalde? I doe embrace your body: How do'ſt thou Sam. And how is't bouncing boyes? O beleeve it, I am much alter'd, much another way: The civil'ſt Gentleman in all your Country: Doe not ye ſee me alter'd? ye, and nay Gentlemen, A much converted man: wher's the beſt wine boyes? What haſt thou made up twenty yet? Look to your skin, Rambaldo the ſleeping Gyant Will rowze, and rent thee piece-meale. Thou never meaneſt then To marry any that thou lov'ſt? Thou haſt been a pretious rogue. What's the matter? Whither goe all theſe men-menders, theſe Phyſitians? Whoſe dog lyes ſicke o'th mulligrubs? Who? yong Frank? The onely temper'd ſpirit, Scholler, Souldier, Courtier: and all in one piece? 'tis not poſſible. Miſtreſſe Alice, I joy to ſee you Lady. And how do'ſt thou? I muſt know, and I will know. But this word. Let rogues be ſtaid that have no habitation, A gentleman may wander: ſit thee down Frank, And ſee what I have brought thee: come diſcover, Open the ſceane, and let the work appeare, A friend at need you rogue is worth a million. Ye are an Aſſe, a twirepipe, A Ieffrey John bo peepe, thou mimiſter, Thou mend a left-handed pack-ſaddle, out puppey, My friend Frank, but a very fooliſh fellow: Do'ſt thou ſee that bottle? view it well. No, no, I have no hope, nor is it fit friends, My life has bin ſo lewd, my looſe condition, Which I repent too late, ſo lamentable, That any thing but curſes light upon me, Exorbitant in all my waies. In all my courſes, cureleſſe diſobedience. No counſell friends, No looke before I leapt. To what end gentlemen, when all is periſh'd Vpon a wrack, is there a hope remaining? The ſea, that nev'r knew ſorrow, may be pittifull, My credit's ſpilt, and ſunke, nor is it poſſible, Were my life lengthened out as long as. I have a vertuous ſiſter, but I ſcorn'd her, A Miſtreſſe too, a noble gentlewoman, For goodneſſe all out-going. Why, I ſhall anſwere it, you fearefull widgen, I ſhall appeare toth' action. With any gentlewoman That ſhall appeare at window: ye may rehearſe too By your commiſſion ſafely, ſome ſweet parcels Of poetry to a Chambermaid. By no meanes, no boyes, I am the man reſerv'd for ayre, 'tis my part, And if ſhe be not rock, my voyce ſhall reach her: Ye may record a little, or ye may whiſtle, As time ſhall miniſter, but for maine ſinging, Pray ye ſatisfie your ſelves: away, be carefull. Nothing but famine frights thee: come hither Fidler, Whad Ballads are you ſeen in beſt: be ſhort ſir. Excellent, Rare matters all. All excellent: No tuning as ye love me; let thy Fidle Speake welch, or any thing that's out of all tune, The vilder ſtill the better, like thy ſelfe, For I preſume thy voyce will make no trees dance. Keep ye to that key, are they all abed trow? I am here Love, tell me deere Love, How I may obtaine thy ſight. The loue of Greece and it tickled him ſo, That he deviſed a way to goe. Now ſing the Duke of Northumberland. O woman: O miſerable woman, I am ſpoil'd, My leg, my leg, my leg, oh both my legs. O I am lam'd for ever: O my leg, Broken in twenty places: O take heed, Take heed of women, Fidler: oh a Surgeon, A Surgeon, or I dye: oh my good people, No charitable people, all deſpightfull, Oh what a miſery am I in: oh my leg. Oh doe not touch it rogue. O my leg. Oh maim'd for ever with a fall, he's ſpoil'd too, I ſee his braines. Oh, Oh. Prethee be quiet, If he play faire play, Come, you muſt helpe me preſently. Nay I'le goe with thee Doll: four hundred a yeere wench. Exeunt. COme quickly, quickly, quickly, paint me handſomly Take heed my noſe be not in graine too, Come Doll, Doll, diſen me. As I am a gentleman: Out with this hayre Doll, handſomely. I wy' not, that I wy' not. Pray hold ſir. Nay then have at ye with a counter-ſpell, From Elves, Hobs and Fayries, that trouble our Dayries, From Fire-drakes and fiends, and ſuch as the divell ſends, Defend us heaven. Exi MOre ſtops yet? ſure the fiend's my ghoſtly father, Old Ʋ alentine: what wind's in his poope? In a Nunnery? That courſe muſt not be ſuffered Maſter Ʋ alentine, Her mother never knew it: rare ſport for me: Sport upon ſport, by th' breake of day I'le meet ye, And feare not man, wee'l have her out I warrant ye, I cannot ſtay now. By no meanes. Good night. This thrives well, Every one takes me for my ſiſter, excellent: This Nunnerys fal ſo pat too, to my figure, Where there be handſome wenches, and they ſhall know it If once I creep in, ere they get me out againe: Stay, her's the houſe and one of her Maids. Still Miſtreſſe Dorothy? this geere will cotton. Where is your Miſtreſſe? Yes, I'le comfort her. I warrant thee I'le warme her. A very rogue, a ranke rogue. Good night, good night wench. I'le play the Mouſe Nan, How cloſe the little thiefe lyes. If it do hang for' Yet ile be quarterd here firſt. Ile kiſſe thee ere I come to bed: ſweet Mary. And view that ſtormy face, that has ſo thundered me, A coldne's crept over't now; by your leave, candle, And next doore by yours too, ſo, a pretty, pretty Shall I now looke upon ye: by this light it moves me. Holy ſaints, defend me. The devill, devill, devill, devill, O the devill. I am abus'd moſt damnedly: moſt beaſtly, Yet if it be a ſhe devill: But the houſe is up, And here's no ſtaying longer in this Caſſock, Woman, I here diſclaime thee; and in vengeance Ile marry with that devill, but ile vex thee. Plague O your ſpaniſh leather hide; ile waken ye: Devill, good night: good night good devill. Rore againe, devill, rore againe. Ex. Tho. I take right ſir: Hylas, are you feretting Ile fit you with a pennyworth preſently. Faith ſir, I do no harme, nor none I looke for Yet I am glad, I have met ſo good a gentleman, Againſt all chances: for though I never knew ye Yet I have heard much good ſpoke of ye, Nay then ye love me not. Not without marriage. Get you afore, and ſtay me at the Chappell, Cloſe by the Nunnery, there you ſhall finde a night Prie •• Little ſir Hugh, and he can ſay the Matrimony Over without booke, for we muſt have no company Nor light, for feare my father know, which muſt not yet And then to morrow night. No, not a bit, I am ſent of buſineſſe About my dowry, ſweet, doe not you ſpoile all now, 'Tis of muh haſte. I can ſcarce ſtay the marriage, Now if you love me, get you gone. A rope kiſſe ye, Come, come, I ſtand o'thornee. Nothing but ſpirit Aunt. Peace, or I'le conjure too Aunt. That's all one, her's my purpoſe: Out with this Nun, ſhe is too handſome for ye, I'le tell thee (Aunt) and I ſpeake it with teares to thee, If thou keptſt her here, as yet I hope thou art wiſer, Mark but the miſchiefe followes. Let her be what ſhe will, ſhe will undoe thee, Let her but one houre out, as I direct ye, Or have among your Nuns againe. Ile make more, if I live Wench Nay doe not looke on me: I care not for ye. You are a truſty husband, And a hot lover too. Stay, or I'le make ye ſtay: come hither ſiſter, Peace a little, Thou would'ſt faine have a wife? Thou ſhalt have a wife, & a fruitful wife, for I find • Hylas known ſon agen. That I ſhall never be able to bring thee children. Thou ſhalt be better Hylas, thou haſt 7 hundred pound a yeer, And thou ſhalt make her 3 hundred joynture. Thou ſhalt boy, and ſhalt beſtow Two hundred pound in clothes, looke on her, A delicate luſty wench, ſhe has fifteen hundred, And ſeaſible: ſtrike hands, or I'le ſtrike firſt. Strike, brother, Hylas quickly, Try that out ſoon, I ſay, my brother Hylas. No, not a bit, you are a vertuous Lady, And love to live in contemplation. The foole ſhall not ride ye, There lye my woman, now my man againe, And now for travell once more. Hold your ſelfe contented: for I ſay I will travell, And ſo long I will travell, till I finde a father That I never knew, and a wife that I never look'd for, And a ſtate without expectation, So reſt you merry gentlemen. This will not doe it, Miſtreſſe, Shall we to Church ſtraight? Away then, faire afore. Exeunt.
Gone diſcontent, it ſeemes. I am gladder to ſee you, with more love too I dare maintaine it, then my fathers ſorry To ſee (as he ſuppoſes) your converſion: And I am ſure he is vext, nay more I know it, He has prai'd againſt it mainely: but it appeares ſir Ye had rather blinde him with that poore opinion, Then in your ſelfe correct it, deereſt brother, Since there is in our uniforme reſemblance, No more to make us two, but our bare ſexes: And ſince one happy birth produced us hither, Let one more happy minde. Leave that trick too, Then doe ſo. For o' my fath ſhe will not ſee your brother. Now you play your true ſelf; How would my father love this! I'le aſſure ye She will not ſee you: ſhe has heard, (and lowdly) The gambolls that you plaid ſince your departure, In every Towne ye came, your ſeverall miſcheifes. Your rowſes, and your wenches: all your quarrells, And the no cauſes of 'em: theſe I take it Although ſhe love ye well, to modeſt eares, To one that waited for your reformation, To which end travell was propounded by her Vncle, Muſt needs, and reaſon for it, be examined, And by her modeſty, and fear'd too light too To fyle with her affections: ye have loſt her For any thing I ſee, exil'd your ſelfe. But how long? No. I: ſwagger. 'Tis not my fault, Come hither, come, do you ſee that clowd that flyes there? So light are you, and blown with every fancy: Will ye but make me hope ye may be civill? I know your nature's ſweet enough, and tender, Not grated on, nor curb'd: doe you love your Miſtreſſe? Would ye ſee her? And appeare to her A thing to be belov'd? Change then A little of your wildeneſſe into wiſedome, And put on a more ſmoothneſſe: I'le doe the beſt I can to helpe ye, yet I doe proteſt ſhe ſwore, and ſwore it deeply, She would never ſee you more: where's your mans heart now? What doe you faint at this? No thought of fighting: Goe in, and there wee'l talke more: be but rul'd, And what lyes in my power, ye ſhall be ſure of. Pray heaven he make it good Alice. O pardon me, deere friend, it was to welcome A brother, that I have ſome cauſe to love well. Not perfect: I hope he will be. Pray do not think ſo, for he loves you deerely, Vpon my troth moſt firmely: would faine ſee you. It may be, Without the loſſe of credit too: he's not Such a prodigious thing, ſo monſtrous, To fling from all ſociety. Deere friend, He was not ſo before he went. And is your hate ſo mortall? I give up that hope then: pray, for your friends ſake, If I have any intereſt within ye, Doe but this courteſie, accept this Letter. The ſame: 'tis but a minutes reading, And as we looke on ſhapes of painted divels, Which for the preſent may diſturb our fancy, But with the next new object looſe 'em, ſo If this be foule, ye may forget it, 'pray: I will not lye: I have not, But I preſume, ſo much he honours you, The worſt part of himſelfe was caſt away When to his beſt part he writ this. J thanke ye deere friend, I know ſhe loves him. What has he writ? Ha, what has the mad man done? What ayle ye? I am ſorry. Out upon him bedlam. I am mad too, And yet can apprehend ye: fare ye well, The foole ſhall now fiſh for himſelfe. Farewell Alice. Exeunt. VVHy do you raile at me? do I dwell in her To force her to do this or that? your Letter, A wilde-fire on your Letter; our ſweet Letter; You are ſo learned in your writs: ye ſtand now As if ye had worried ſheepe: you muſt tutne tippet, And ſuddenly, and truely, and diſcreetly Put on the ſhape of order and humanity, Or you muſt marry Malkyn the May Lady: You muſt, deere brother: doe you make me carrier Of your confound-mee's, and your culverings? Am I a ſeemely agent for your othes? Who would have writ ſuch a deboſh'd? In blaſphemies? Rack a maids tender cares, with dam's and divels? Take your owne courſe For I ſee all perſwaſion's loſt upon ye: Humanitie, all drownd: from this howre fayrely No, if I were, deere brother I would keep you company: get a new Miſtreſſe Som ſuburb Sant, that ſix pence, and ſom others Will draw to parley: carowſe her health in Cans And candles ends, and quarrell for her beauty, Such a ſweet hart muſt ſerve your turne: your old love Releaſes ye of all your tyes; diſclaimes ye And utterly abjures your memory Till time has better mannag'd ye, will ye comand me Any worthy ſervice Vnto my father ſir, that I may tell him Even to his peace of heart, and much rejoycing Ye are his true ſon Thom ſtill? will it pleaſe ye To beat ſome halfe a dozen of his ſervants preſently That I may teſtifie you have brought the ſame faith Vnblemiſhd home, ye carried out? or if it like you There be two chambermaids within, yong wenches, Handſom and apt for exerciſe: you have bin good, ſir, And charitable though I ſay it Signiour To ſuch poore orphans: and now, by th' way I think on't Your yong reare Admirall, I meane your laſt baſtard Don Iohn, ye had by Lady Blanch the Dairy Maid, Is by an Academy of learned Gypſies, Foreſeeing ſome ſtrange wonder in the infant Stolne from the Nurſe, and wanders with thoſe Prophets. There is plate in the parlour, and good ſtore ſir, When your wants ſhall ſupply it. So moſt humbly (Firſt rendring my due ſervice) I take leave ſir. Exit. You have a ſonne Sir. Your ſelfe. Diſpaire not I do beſeech you Sir, nor tempt your weakneſſe, For if you like it ſo, I can aſſure you He is the ſame man ſtill. You never Sir, So will I know my duty: and for heaven ſake, Take but this councell with ye ere you marry, You were wont to beare me: take him, and confeſſe him Search him toth' quicke, and if you find him faile Do as pleaſe you; a Mothers name I honour. Heer's fine ſport. And yet you like it Was ever ſinne ſo glorious? Now our upon thee Monſter. Why do you lye ſo damnably, ſo fooliſhly? Was ever ſuch a wilde Aſſe? And do'ſt thou think men will not beat thee monſtrouſly For abuſing their wives and children? I wonder at thee. How ſtand ye with your miſtreſſe? I diſcard ye. I'le no hand with ye, No bawd to your abuſes. Thou never knew'ſt that road: I heare your vigile You may come in to dinner, and I'le anſwere ye. If you ſhould play now Your divels parts againe. O feirce villaine. You had beſt try him. O, for gentle Nicholas. And I a Waſtcoate, Wench. They muſt needs Mall: for 'tis a pricking age grown Prethee to bed, for I am monſtrous ſleepy. Would I were Wench, You ſhould heare further. IN troth ſir, you never ſpoke to me. I ſaw ye not theſe two dayes. 'Tis true I was there, But that I ſaw or ſpoke to you. Pray ſir be ſatisfi'd, And wherein I can doe you good, command me, What a mad foole is this? ſtay here a while ſir, Whilſt we walke in, and make your peace. Exit. Nay you may thanke your ſelfe, 'twas your owne ſtructures. Good morrow to you ſir. Would ye ought with us, gentlemen? Your will ſir. How ſir? Iewels ſir? Who are you? The man's fooliſh Sir, you looke ſoberly: who is this fellow, And where's his buſineſſe? Came ye out of Bedlam? Alas, tis ill ſir, that ye ſuffer him To walke in th' open ayre thus: 'twill undoe hlm. A pretty hanſome gentleman: great pitty. Did not I ſay he was mad? By th' mas, ſhe muſt ſir. For ile no husband here, before I know him: And ſo good morrow to ye: Come, let's goe ſeeke'em. You have made brave ſport. In truth like him. You'l let me like? If you can pleaſe me. Then you muſt allow me another ſervant.
'Tis moſt certaine I have now heard all, and all the truth. You look far better truſt me, the freſh colour Creeps now againe into his cheeks. Indeed it do's ye harme ſir. This ayre ſir laying now ſeaſon'd ye: will keep ye ever. Sure, I know that voyce well. O that this could be truth. I like this well. Well Tom My Tom againe, if this be truth. Now heaven defend. Say you ſo Sir. And are ye there my Iuggler Away we are abus'd Alice. A greaſe pot guild your fidle ſtrings: how do you, How is my deere? Are ye ſo crafty ſir? I ſhall meet with ye, I knew your tricke, and I was willing: my Tom, Mine owne Tom, now to ſatisfie thee, welcome, welcome, Welcome my beſt friend to me, all my deereſt. I thinke they are all gone. And you as craftily. Come, let's goe in then lovingly: O my Skarfe Tom. I loſt it thereabout, finde it, and weare it As your poore Miſtreſſe favour. Exit. One parting word ſweet Thomas, Though to ſave your credit, I diſcharg'd your Fidler, I muſt not ſatisfie your folly too ſir, Ye'are ſubtle, but beleeve it Foxe, i'le finde ye, The Surgeons will be here ſtrait, rore againe boy, And breake thy legs for ſhame, thou wilt be ſport elſe, Good night. Let the light ſtand far enough. Stay you to entertaine him to his chamber, But keep cloſe wench, he flyes at all. Peace for ſhame. Prethee leave laughing. Out upon ye Thomas What do ye meane to do? ile call the houſe up, O god, I am ſure ye will not, ſhall not ſerve ye, For up ye goe now, and ye were my Father. Your courage wilbe cold anon. What would he do indeed Doll? Prethee leave laughing. Much good may it do you ſir. Dor. Ha, ha, ha, ha, the devill O the devill. Byr' Lady, but you ſhall not ſir, ile watch ye. Open the doores before him: let him vaniſh. Now, let him come againe, ile uſe him kinder How now Wench. What ſaid he to thee. Alas poore Kate; ile give thee a new Petticoate, Draw in the bed Maides, And ſee it made againe; put freſh ſheetes on too, For Doll. and I: come Wench, lets laugh an houre now, To morrow earely, will wee ſee yong Cellide They ſay ſhe has taken Sanctuary: love, & they Are thicke ſowne, but come up ſo full of thiſtles. A match, but art not thou thy brother? Come, no more of that Doll. Exeunt. VVHat a coyle has this Fellow kept i'th' Nunnery Sure he has run the Abbeſſe out of her wits. To what ſir? Good ſir, goe ſleepe: for if I credit have She was in my armes, then, abed. Vpon my troth exceeding like, Now ſir, for you & I to make the feaſt full. Come foole, I am friends now. And I next. You ſhall not Vpon my faith, I love you now extremely, And now J'le kiſſe ye. Why when we are married, we'l doe more,
INdeed he's much chang'd, extreamely alter'd, His colour faded ſtrangely too.
