You cannot be the maſter of your health, Either ſome feaver lyes in wait to catch ye, Whoſe harbinger's already in your face We ſee preparing: or ſome diſcontent, Which if it lye in this houſe, I dare ſay Both for this noble Gentleman, and all That live within it, ſhall as readily Be purg'd away, and with as much care ſoften'd, And where the cauſe is. And this ſhall be the laſt fit. Be of good cheere Sir. Me thinks he ſhould goe neere it, if he love her; If ſhe love him Moſt truly: Nay were it my ſelfe, at your entreaty. So dutifull; Becauſe you urge it ſir, It is in deed, I know it. And now know how ye love me. By your leave Gentlemen: And pray ye your leave a while too, I have ſomething Of ſecret to imparr unto the patient. You ſhall not ſtay for me. How do you worthy Sir? Yes; and do more then that too: comfort ye I ſee ye have need. I would be ſorry ſir, my charity And my good wiſhes for your health ſhould merit So ſtubborn • a conſtruction: will it pleaſe ye To taſte a little of this Cordiall Enter Valentine. For this I thinke muſt cure ye. Do you not underſtand? of this, this Cordiall. Do not wonder: For tis not impudence, nor want of honour Makes me do this: but love to ſave your life ſir Your life, too excellent to looſe in wiſhes Love, virtuous love. Do not diſpaire: nor do not thinke to boldly I dare abuſe my promiſe, t'was your friends And ſo faſt tyde, I thought no time could ruine: But ſo much has your danger, and that ſpell The powerfull name of friend, prevail'd above him To whom I ever owe obedience, That here I am, by his command to cure ye, Nay more for ever, by his full reſignement And willingly I ratefie it. Pray tell me If I had never knowne that gentleman Would you not willingly embrace my offer? And can ye be unwilling He being old and impotent: his aime too Levell'd at you, for your good? not conſtrain'd, But out of cure, and councell? alas conſider Play but the woman with me, and conſider As he himſelfe do's, and I now dare ſee it Truly conſider ſir, what miſery. What loſſe of youth, What everlaſting baniſhment from that Our yeares doe only covet to arive at Equall affections and ſhot together: What living name can dead age leave behind him What art of memory but fruitleſſe doating? To you unleſſe ye apply it With more and firmer faith, and ſo digeſt it I ſpeake but of things poſſible, not done Nor like to be, a poſſet cures your ſickneſſe And yet I know ye grieve this; and howſoever The worthines of Friend may make ye ſtagger Which is a faire thing in ye, yet my Patient, My gentle Patient, I would faine ſay more If you would underſtand. Yet ſure your ſickneſſe is not ſo forgetfull Nor you ſo willing to be loſt. Do not rave Sir, Nor let the violence of thoughts diſtract ye, You ſhall enjoy me: I am yours: I pitty By thoſe faire eyes I do. With all my ſoule poſſeſſe her. Exit, Val. Till this minut. I ſcorn'd, and hated ye, and came to coſen ye: Vtter'd thoſe things might draw a wonder on me, To make ye mad. Nor did your danger, but in charity. Move me a whit: nor you appeare unto me More then a common object, yet, now truely, Truely, and nobly I doe love ye deerely, And from this houre, ye are the man I honour, You are the man, the excellence, the honeſty, The onely friend, and I am glad your ſickneſſe Fell ſo moſt happily at this time on ye, To make this truth the worlds. Backe to your honeſty, make that good ever, 'Tis like a ſtrong built Caſtle, ſeated high, That drawes on all ambitions, ſtill repaire it, Still fortifie it: there are thouſand foes Beſides the tyrant beauty, will aſſaile it: Looke to your Centin is that watch it hourely, Your eyes, let them not wander. Or do's ſhe play ſtill with me? Keep your eares, The two maine ports that may betray ye ſtrongly From light beliefe firſt, then from flattery, Eſpecially where woman beats the parley: The body of your ſtrength, your noble heart From ever yeelding ro diſhoneſt ends, Rigd round about with vertue, that no breaches, No ſubtle mynes may meet ye. What are ye? ſpeake, ſpeake gently, And next, what would ye with me? You are no woman certaine. I muſt obey your will. Though much unwilling, you have made me yeeld, More for his ſake I ſee: how full of ſorrow Sweet catching ſorrow, he appeares? O love, That thou but knew'ſt to heale, as well as hurt us. O where have I beſtrew'd my faith: in neither: Let's in for ever now, there is vertue. In, good Mother.
Put up your booke ſir, We are all undone elſe. Ye have utterly undone: cleane diſcharg'd me, I am for the ragged regiment. O pardon me. I know him but too well: eight ſcore I take it Will not keepe me from beating, if not killing: I'le give him leave to breake a leg, and thank him: You might have ſav'd all this, and ſworn a little. What had an oath or two bin? or a head broke, Though t'had been mine, to have ſatisſied the old man? Now 'tis too late, I take it: Will ye be drunk to night, (a leſſe intreaty Has ſerv'd your turne) and ſave all yet? not mad drunk, For then ye are the divell, yet the drunker, The better for your father ſtill: your ſtate is deſperate, And with a deſperate cure ye muſt recover it: Doe ſomething, doe ſir: doe ſome drunken thing, Some mad thing, or ſome any thing to help us. I'th Lodge, alone ſir, None but her owne attendants. Via. Exit.
The ſame Sam ſtill: your friend ſir. He nev'r perceives 'em Longer then looking on. Why you may take a Maid. Onely his eyes: and O my conſcience They lye with half the kingdome. O the Gentleman, The yong ſmug Signiour, Maſter Ʋ alentine, Brought out of travell with him, as J heare Is falne ſick o'th ſudden, deſperate ſicke, And likely they goe thither. Ther's one can better ſatisfie you. Never looke ſo narrowly, the mark's in her mouth ſtill, Pray ſir be temperate, You know your owne ſtate beſt. A learned queſtion: Or grant the diaphragm • by a rupture, The ſigne being then in the head of Capricorne. And we'l be gone all together. Be rul'd though. Your minde is too miſtruſtfull. Thou haſt her. Not I. At your will ſir. Exit Hyl. & Sam. You muſt be courting wenches Through key-holes, Captain Hylas, come and be comforted, The skin is ſcarce broke. How doe ye ſir? Here's a night indeed. Thou hadſt as good be quiet, for o' my conſcience He'l put another on thee elſe. Thou art ever ready To thruſt thy ſelfe into theſe ſhe occaſions, And he as full of knavery to accept it. That will not be amiſſe, but to fight with him Is to no purpoſe: beſides, he's truely valiant, And a moſt deadly hand: thou never foughtſt yet, Not o' my conſcience haſt no faith in fighting. To pay him with a project: Watch him too, I would wiſh ye: prethee tell me, Do'ſt thou affect theſe women ſtill? Doſt thou love any woman? Of any age too? And defect too? 'Tis well ſir, Ye make ſo worthy uſes: but quid igitur, What ſhall we now determine? Let's finde him firſt, he'l quickly give occaſion, But take heed to your ſelfe, and ſay I warn'd ye: He has a plaguy pate. VVHere haſt thou been man? What's the matter? Thou art not married? To whom prethee? I thought there was ſome ſuch trick in't, you ſtole from me But who, for heaven ſake? But who Hylas? Who, Monſieur Thomas? O now I ſmell ye Hylas. Do's he know of it? Is there no tricke in't? She's a brave wench. Take heed Hylas, Why there's the gentlewoman, How ſtrange ſhe beares it? By heaven, thou art abus'd ſtill. Let me not live more if thou be'ſt not cozens, I told ye. I told ye what ye had done. What doe all theſe here? J ſtill told ye. Take her, and uſe her well, ſhe's a brave gentlewoman.
A Pluriſie. I ſee it. CLap on the Cataplaſme. Are the things ready? And is the Barber come? Bring out the oyles then. We are abus'd ſirs.
speeches.2: I rather hold it For tremor cordis. Now with your favours, J ſhould think a vomit: For take away the cauſe, the effect muſt follow, The ſtomack's foule and fur'd, the pot's unflam'd yet. He ſhall doe well my friend. And ſee thoſe brothe • there, Ready within this houre, pray keep your armes in, The ayre is raw, and miniſters much evill. How doe ye? 'Tis dangerous, For now his fancy turnes too.
speeches.3: Doe you marke the Pheſes? 'Tis a moſt peſtilent contagious feaver, A ſurfet, a plaguy ſurfet: he muſt bleed. I ſay bleed. No, no, wee'l rectifie that part by milde meanes, Nature ſo ſunke, muſt finde no violence. Ther's no doubt in him, none at all, nev'r feare him. Pray be rul'd ſir. A great diſtemper, it growes hotter ſtill. I mary ſuch a Phyſicke May chance to find the humour: be not long Lady For we muſt miniſter within this halfe houre. Exit. Plus. Drinke hard Gentlemen, And get unwholeſome drabs: 'tis ten to one then We ſhall heare further from ye; your note alter'd. Ex.
speeches.1: By no meanes. I ſay 'tis dangerous: The perſon being ſpent ſo much before hand, And nature drawne ſo low, clyſters, coole clyſters. Come, we will attend him. Excellent well I warrant thee, right and ſtraight friend. Bring in the Lettice cap: you muſt be ſhaved ſir, And then how ſuddenly wee'l make you ſleep. Open your mouth I pray ſir. Withall our hearts.
Wilt pleaſe ye draw neere? the weake gentleman Growes worſe and worſe ſtill. My maſters love ſir. An houre agoe ſir. Sir, the yong Gentlewomen Sent me to ſee what company ye had with ye They much deſire to viſite ye. Yes ſir. Miſtreſſe Alice. I doe not thinke ſhe do's. You have ty'd my tongue up. Exit. Do you call Sir? I will not faile Sir. Who's there? what noyſe is this? what rogue At theſe houres? So the Groome delivers Somewhat before the breake of day. As a pie Sir: I am ſure I heard it. No, but one Fidle; But twenty noyces. Enter Launcelet. The beſt deviſes ſir: her's my fellow Launcelet He can informe ye all: he was among 'em, A mad thing too: I ſtood but in a corner. He will ſir. Enter Thomas. By theſe ten bones ſir, if theſe eies, and eares Can heare and ſee. Did you not take two Wenches from the Watch too And put 'em into pudding lane? He's not at home ſir, His ſiſter thinks he's gone to th' Nunnery, Yes ſir. Exeunt.
THat he is deſp • rate ſick, I do beleeve well, And that without a ſp • edy cure, it kils him, But that it lyes within the help • of phyſicke, Now to reſtore his health, or art to cure him: Beleeve it you are coſened: cleane beſide it. I would tell ye the true cauſe too, but 'twould vexe ye, Nay, run ye mad. Now I perceive ye ſo well ſet, I'le tell you, Hei mihi quod nullis amor, eſt medicabilis herbis. 'Twill prove too certaine, But beare it nobly ſir, youth hath his errors. Good morrow Signieur. My good neighbour, Me thinks you are ſtirring early ſince your travell, You have learn'd the rule of health ſir, where's your miſtres? She keeps her warme I warrant ye, a bed yet? Did you lye with her Lady? When laſt ſaw ye her? Was ſhe abed then? I have been ſtrangely haunted with a dreame All this long night, and after many wakings, The ſame dreame ſtill; me thought I met yong Cellide Iuſt at S. Katherines gate the Nunnery. Her face ſlubber'd o're with teares, and troubles, Me thought ſhe cry'd unto the Lady Abbeſſe, For charity receive me holy woman, A Maid that has forgot the worlds affections, Into thy virgin order: me thought ſhe tooke her, Put on a Stole, and ſacred robe upon her, And there I left her. Good Miſtreſſe Alice Doe me the favour (yet to ſatisfie me) To ſtep but up, and ſee. You know not my dreames, They are unhappy ones, and often truths, But this I hope, yet Neighbours, how do's the gentleman? How found ye my words About the nature of his ſickneſſe Valentine? Alas poore gentleman. Ye promis'd me ſir to beare all theſe croſſes. But nobly, Truely to weigh, It muſt be truth ſhe tels ye, And now I'le ſhew ye why I came: this morning A man of mine being employed about buſineſſe, Came early home, who at S. Katherines Nunnery, About day peep told me he met your Miſtreſſe, And as I ſpoke it in a dreame, ſo troubled And ſo received by the • bbeſſe, did he ſee her? The wonder made me riſe, and haſte unto ye To know the cauſe. I will not Lady. We ſhall know ſhortly more, apply your own care At home good Alice, a • d truſt him to my counſell. Nay, doe not weep, all ſhall be well, deſpaire not. Exeunt. GOod ſir go back again, and take my counſell, Sores are not cur'd by ſorrows, nor time broke from us, Pul'd back again by ſighes. Doe that that may redeeme ye, goe back quickly, Sebaſtians daughter can prevaile much with her, The Abbeſſe is her Aunt too. Content ye, That ſhall be my taske if he be alive, Or where my travell and my care may reach him, I'le bring him backe againe. So ſuddenly She cannot, haſte ye therefore inſtantly away ſir, To put that daughter by firſt as to a father, Then as a friend ſhe was committed to ye, And all the care ſhe now has: by which priviledge She cannot doe her this violence, But you may breake it, and the law allowes ye. Leave diſputing Againſt your ſelfe, if you will needs be miſerable Spight of her goodneſſe, and your friends perſwaſions, Thinke on, and thrive thereafter. No more, I know your ſoul's divided Valentine, Cure but that part at home with ſpeedy marriage Ere my returne, for then thoſe thoughts that vext her, While there ran any ſtreame for looſe affections, Will be ſtopt up, and chaſte ey'd honour guide her Away, and hope the beſt ſtill: I'le worke for ye, And pray too heartily, away, no more words Exeunt. Theſe call for paſſengers, I'le ſtay, & ſee What men they take aboard. Ha, 'tis not much unlike him. 'Tis he, I know 'tis he now. Be not ſo quicke ſit: Saylors I here charge ye By vertue of this warrant, as you will anſwer it, For both your ſhip and Merchant I know perfectly: Lay hold upon this fellow. J ſir. Ye have rob'd a gentleman, One that ye are bound to for your life and being: Money and horſe unjuſtly ye tooke from him, And ſomething of more note, but for y'are a gentleman. Guard him to'th water, I charge you Saylors, there I will receive him, And backe convey him to a Iuſtice. COme ſir, for this night I ſhall entertaine ye, And like a gentleman, how ere your fortune Hath caſt ye on the worſt part. I am angry with my ſelfe now For putting this forc'd way upon his patience, Yet any other courſe had been too ſlender: Yet what to thinke I know not, for moſt liberally He hath confeſs'd ſtrange wronge, which if they prove ſo, How ere the others long love may forget all, Yet 'twas moſt fit he ſhould come back, and this way Drinke that: and now to my care leave your priſoner, I'le be his guard for this night. Good night my honeſt friends: Come ſir, I hope There ſhall be no ſuch cauſe of ſuch a ſadneſſe As you put on. A conſtant gentleman: would I had taken A feaver when I took this harſh way to diſturb him, Come walke with me ſir, ere to morrow night I doubt not but to ſee all this blown over. Exeunt. HA'ſt thou inquir'd him out? Moſt likely: I'le away, an houre hence ſirha, Come you along with this yong gentleman, Doe him all ſervice, and faire office. I Have brought him backe againe. Would he had ſo too. When al's tryde I feare you'l change your faith: bring in the gentleman. Be ruld by me: I ſee her eye faſt on him: And what ye heard, beleeve, for tis ſo certaine He neither dar'd, nor muſt oppoſe my evidence; And be you wiſe, yong Lady, and beleeve too. This man you love, Sir? This man you put into a free poſſeſſion Of what his wants could aske: or your ſelfe render? Nay do not wonder at it, he ſhall ſay it, Are ye not guiltie thus? To give a proofe I ſpeake not enviouſly Looke here: do you know theſe Iewels. Beſhrew me, But much: and maine reſemblance, both of face And lineaments of body: now heaven grant it. 'Tis true, beleeve her ſir, and we all joy with ye.

O my deareſt, Let but your goodneſſe judge: your owne part: pitiy: Set but your eyes on his afflictions: He is mine, and ſo becomes your charge: but thinke What ruine nature ſuffers in this yong man, What loſſe humanity, and noble manhood: Take to your better judgement my declining, My age, hung full of impotence, and ils, My body budding now no more: ſeere winter Hath ſeal'd that ſap up, at the beſt and happieſt I can but be your infant: you my nurſe, And how unequall deereſt: where his yeeres, His ſweetneſſe, and his ever ſpring of goodneſſe, My fortunes growing in him, and my ſelfe too, Which makes him all your old love: miſconceive not, I ſay not this, as weary of my bondage, Or ready to infringe my faith: beare witneſſe, Thoſe eyes that I adore ſtill, thoſe lamps that light me To all the joy I have.

So it is, and well conſider'd, The ſecond, for 'tis fil'd with broken Greek ſir, Which will ſo tumble in his ſtomacke, Doctor, And worke upon the crudities, conceive me The feares, and the fidle ſtrings within it, That thoſe damn'd ſoules muſt diſembogue againe. Right ſir. Ever. Satis feciſti domine: my laſt cauſe, My laſt is, and not leaſt, moſt learned Doctors, Becauſe in moſt Phyſitians heads (I meane thoſe That are moſt excellent, and old withall, And angry, though a patient ſay his prayers, And Paracelſians that doe trade with poyſons, We have it by tradition of great writers) There is a kinde of toad-ſtone bread, whoſe vertue The Doctor being dri'd. Meet with the paſſion Hupercondriaca, And ſo cauſe a carnoſitie in the kidneyes. Muſt not the brains being butter'd with this humour Anſwer me that. And wilt thou be gone ſaies one? Come hither Crab, What gentlewomen are theſe? my Miſtreſſe? Harke ye ſirha. No word of my being here, unleſſe ſhe know it. Take that, and mum, then Sit you downe good Francis, And not a word of me till ye heare from me, And as you finde my humour, follow it: You two come hither, and ſtand cloſe, unſeen boyes, And doe as I ſhall tutor ye. Prethee no more, but helpe me now, Talke with the gentlewomen? Of what forſooth? whoſe maiden-head the laſt maske Suffer'd impreſſion, or whoſe clyſter wrought beſt: Take me as I ſhall tell thee. Your wee zell face muſt needs be ferretting About the farthing-ale, Doe as I bid ye, Or by this light. Stand cloſe and marke me, O my fortune, But it is juſt, I be deſpis'd and hated. O I ſhall die. Come lead me to my Friend to take his farewell, And then what fortune ſhall befall me, welcome. How do's it ſhow? Where is ſhe. This was thy Rouging. For thou wert ever whiſpering: fye upon thee Now could I breeks thy head. Do not anger me, For by this hand ile beate the buzard blind then She ſhall not ſcape me thus: farewell for this time, Thou ſhalt along too, for I meane to plague thee For this nights ſins, I will nev'r leave walking of thee Till I have worne thee out. You will not leave me Sam. KEepe you the backe doore there, and be ſure None of her ſervants enter, or goe out, If any woman paſſe, ſhe is lawfull prize, boyes Cut off all convoyes. That's as ye think good your ſelves: if you deſerve it, Why 'tis the eaſieſt thing to compaſſe: beaten? What bugbeares dwell in thy brains? who ſhould beat thee? Rare ſtill. Come ſtrike up then: and ſay the Merchants daughter, We'l beare the burthen: proceed to inciſion Fidler. Song. Why well I thank ye ſweet heart, Shall we walke in, for now ther's none to trouble us? Now ye are my noble Miſtreſſe: we looſe time ſweet. All, ye did wiſely. We are well met Miſtreſſe. I am made now, I ſee no venture is in no hand: I have it, How now? the doore lock't, and ſhe in before? Am I ſo trim'd? She ſaies moſt true, I muſt not ſtay: ſhe has bobd me, Which if I live, I'le recompence, and ſhortly, Now for a Ballad to bring me off againe. All yong men be warn'd by me, how you do goe a wooing. Seek not to climb, for feare ye fall thereby, comes your undoing, & Exeunt. Away knave, Ye keepe a company of ſawcy fellowes Deboſh'd, & dai • y drunkards, to deavoure ye, Things, whoſe dull ſoules, tend to the Celler only, Ye are ill advis'd ſir, to commit your credit. Tis ſtrange theſe varlets. Extreame ſtrange, ſhould thus boldly Bud in your ſight, unto your ſonne. I touch Authoritie ye raſcall? I violate the Law? O ſtrange impudence? I do beſeech you ſir give no ſuch licence To knaves and drunkards, to abuſe your ſonne thus: Be wiſe in time, and turne'em off: we live ſir In a State govern'd civilly, and ſoberly Where each mans actions ſhould confirme the Law, Not cracke, and canzell it. Purge me'em all ſir. Even as you pleaſe ſir. Tis moſt fit ſir. At your pleaſure. You ſay right ſir. At your diſpoſe: and I beſeech ye too ſir, Fot the word civill, and more ſetled courſe It may be put to uſe, that on the intereſt Like a poore Gentleman. So much for that then. Will you chooſe there ſir? I have. How, is not ſeemely here to ſay. I will: and to the purpoſe; even with all ſir. All ſurely ſir. Her will was fifteene ſir, Her husband is recover'd. Still hoping of your pardon. Do'ſt thou long to have thy head broke? hold thy peace And doe as I would have thee, or by this hand I'le kill thy Parrat, hang up thy ſmall hand, And drinke away thy dowry to a penny. And do'ſt thou thinke Mens wives and children can be abus'd too much? Nay, thou ſhalt adjure me Before I have done. Thou ſhalt not ſleep nor eate. Sweet honey Doll, if I doe not marry her, Honeſtly marry her, if I meane not honourably, Come, thou ſhalt help me, take heed how you vex me, I'le help thee to a husband too, a fine gentleman, I know thou art mad, a tall yong man, a brown man, I ſweare he has his maidenhead, a rich man. Yea and nay Dorothy. I prethee away, thou know'ſt I am monſtrous tickliſh, What do'ſt thou think I love to blaſt my buttocks? On with my Muffler. In what a figure The little foole has pull'd it ſelfe together: Anone you will lye ſtreighter: Ha, ther's rare circumſtance Belongs to ſuch a treatiſe: doe ye tumble, I'le tumble with ye ſtraight wench: ſhe ſleeps ſoundly, Full little thinkſt thou of thy joy that's comming, The ſweet, ſweet joy, full little of the kiſſes, But thoſe unthought of things come ever happieſt. How ſoft the rogue feeles? Oye little villaine, Ye delicate coy thiefe, how I ſhall thrum ye? Your fy away, good ſervant, as ye are a gentleman. I muſt confeſſe, I have long deſir'd your ſight ſir.
